docs.title: Coding Labs
docs.text:
A hands-on, code-first companion track that runs parallel to the course. For each week of Andrew Ng's specialization, the matching lab here shows you how to actually implement the ideas — first from scratch so you see the machinery, then the fast, idiomatic library way you'd really use on the job.

The theory pages teach you what a model is and why it works. These labs teach you how to build one.

docs.title: How to use these
docs.text:
• Read the matching theory lesson first (each lab links back to it), then work the lab.
  • Every code block has a copy button — paste it into a Python file, a Jupyter/Colab notebook, or the terminal and run it as you read. Nothing here is magic; run everything.
  • Labs build in one direction: from scratch → then the library. Don't skip the from-scratch part — it's where the intuition lives.

docs.title: What you'll need
docs.text:
pip install numpy scikit-learn matplotlib     # the classical-ML labs
pip install torch                             # only for the neural-network labs

docs.title: A note on frameworks
docs.text:
• Classical ML (regression, logistic regression, trees, k-means, PCA, anomaly detection — most of the course) is NumPy + scikit-learn. No deep-learning framework involved, and nothing here depends on which one you pick.
  • Neural networks / deep learning use PyTorch, which is today's industry standard. Ng's lectures demonstrate these in TensorFlow/Keras; where that happens, the lab adds a short bridge note — the concepts are identical, only the library syntax differs.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
These labs are grounded in two standard references (rewritten in our own words, not copied):

  • Aurélien Géron — Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch (2025). The beginner-friendly narrator; our primary tutorial voice.
  • Sebastian Raschka et al. — Machine Learning with PyTorch and Scikit-Learn (2022). The from-scratch engineer; our reference for building algorithms up from the math.

Plus Andrew Ng's own optional DeepLearning.AI labs, which pair with each lesson.

docs.title: C1 · W1 — Linear Regression, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 1 · Week 1 lessons that the code builds on — the model, the cost, and gradient descent:

  • Linear Regression Model
  • The Cost Function
  • Gradient Descent → for Linear Regression → Running Gradient Descent

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

You've seen the idea: fit a straight line through your data, then read predictions off the line. Now let's build it three ways, from the inside out:

  1. From scratch, the closed-form way — one matrix equation that jumps straight to the best line.
  2. From scratch, the iterative way — gradient descent, the same "roll downhill" engine you'll reuse for every model later, neural networks included.
  3. The library way — scikit-learn, in three lines, which is what you'd actually type on the job.

All three land on the same line. Seeing why is the whole point.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
We'll generate data that follows a known line — price = 4 + 3 × size — plus random noise, so we can check whether our code recovers the 4 and the 3.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)          # fixed seed → reproducible "random" data
m = 100                                   # number of training examples
X = 2 * rng.random((m, 1))               # feature: house size (m rows, 1 column)
y = 4 + 3 * X + rng.standard_normal((m, 1))   # target: price = 4 + 3·size + noise

X is a column of sizes; y is a column of prices. In the notation from the lesson, m = 100, each row is one training example (x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾).

docs.title: 1. The model as code
docs.text:
The lesson's model is f(x) = w·x + b. Written for many features at once it's a weighted sum plus a bias — which is just a dot product. The standard trick that makes the code clean is to bolt a column of 1s onto X, so the bias b becomes "the weight on a feature that's always 1." Then prediction for the whole dataset is one matrix multiply:

X_b = np.c_[np.ones((m, 1)), X]          # prepend x0 = 1 to every row (the bias column)

def predict(X_b, theta):
    return X_b @ theta                   # ŷ = X · θ   (θ = [b, w])

Here theta holds both parameters: theta[0] is the bias b, theta[1] is the weight w. The @ operator is matrix multiplication.

docs.title: 2. Measuring how good a line is: the cost
docs.text:
Training means finding the theta that fits best — so we need a number for "how bad is this line." That's the mean squared error (the same squared-error cost from the lesson, and the red bars you saw in the interactive):

def mse(X_b, y, theta):
    errors = X_b @ theta - y             # residual for each point: prediction − truth
    return float((errors.T @ errors) / len(y))   # mean of the squared residuals

Lower is better. Every method below is just a different way to make this number as small as possible.

docs.title: 3. Route A — the closed-form solution (the normal equation)
docs.text:
For linear regression there's a beautiful shortcut: a single equation that computes the best theta directly, no iteration. It's called the normal equation:

\[\theta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\] 
theta_best = np.linalg.inv(X_b.T @ X_b) @ X_b.T @ y
print(theta_best.ravel())        # → about [3.9, 3.0]: it recovered the 4 and the 3

That's it — the exact best-fit line in one line of algebra. (The values aren't exactly 4 and 3 because the noise makes the original parameters impossible to recover perfectly; the smaller and noisier the data, the further off they'll be.)

So why ever do anything more complicated? Because inverting Xᵀ X gets slow as the number of features grows, and it breaks down entirely for the huge, many-feature problems (and non-linear models like neural nets) you'll hit later. For those we need a method that scales — gradient descent.

docs.title: 4. Route B — gradient descent, from scratch
docs.text:
Here's the mental picture Géron uses: you're lost on a mountain in thick fog, and you want the valley bottom. You can't see the whole landscape — but you can feel the slope under your feet. So you take a small step in the steepest downhill direction, and repeat. That's gradient descent. The "landscape" is the cost function; the "valley bottom" is the best theta.

The slope of the cost with respect to the parameters is its gradient. For the MSE it works out to a clean formula, and each step nudges theta a little way downhill:

eta = 0.1                                 # learning rate = how big each step is
n_epochs = 1000                           # how many steps to take
theta = rng.standard_normal((2, 1))       # start from a random line

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    gradients = 2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y)   # which way is downhill (for both params)
    theta = theta - eta * gradients                 # take a step that way

print(theta.ravel())          # → the same ~[3.9, 3.0] the normal equation found!

One full pass over the data is called an epoch. After enough epochs, theta settles at the bottom of the bowl — the same answer as Route A. Gradient descent just walked there instead of teleporting.

docs.title: Feel the learning rate
docs.text:
The learning rate eta is the one knob you'll tune constantly. It's exactly the "learning rate" idea from the lesson:

  • Too small → tiny steps, painfully slow to converge (try eta = 0.001).
  • Too large → you overshoot the valley and bounce up the far side; the numbers blow up to nan (try eta = 1.5).
  • Just right → converges in a handful of epochs.
for eta in (0.001, 0.1, 1.5):
    theta = rng.standard_normal((2, 1))
    for _ in range(50):
        theta = theta - eta * (2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y))
    print(f"eta={eta}: theta={theta.ravel()}, cost={mse(X_b, y, theta):.3f}")

Watch the cost for each: small eta is still far off after 50 steps, big eta has diverged, the middle one has nailed it. This exact trade-off shows up for every model you'll train.

Why this matters later: the normal equation only works for linear regression. Gradient descent works for anything you can measure a cost and a slope on — logistic regression, neural networks, all of it. This little loop is the engine of modern ML in miniature.

docs.title: 5. The library way — scikit-learn
docs.text:
In real work you don't hand-roll any of the above. scikit-learn does it in three lines, and it uses a numerically robust method (SVD) under the hood:

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

lin_reg = LinearRegression()
lin_reg.fit(X, y)
print(lin_reg.intercept_, lin_reg.coef_)     # same bias and weight, ~[3.9] and ~[3.0]

Notice scikit-learn keeps the bias (intercept_) separate from the weights (coef_) — so you don't prepend the column of 1s; fit() handles that. Predict on new sizes with lin_reg.predict([[1.5]]).

For very large datasets where even that is too slow, scikit-learn's SGDRegressor runs stochastic gradient descent (one example at a time) — the scaled-up cousin of the loop you wrote in Route B.

docs.title: 6. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code you already ran above, meant to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away if you get stuck. Do at least the first two.

1. Confirm all three agree. Print theta_best, the gradient-descent theta, and scikit-learn's [intercept_, coef_] side by side. Are they the same to 2 decimals?

Solution 
print("normal eq:", theta_best.ravel())
print("grad desc:", theta.ravel())
print("sklearn  :", np.r_[lin_reg.intercept_.ravel(), lin_reg.coef_.ravel()])
# all three ≈ [3.9, 3.0]

2. Add an outlier and re-fit. Append one extreme point, then recompute with the normal equation and compare. This is the leverage effect from the interactive, now in code.

Solution 
X_out = np.r_[X_b, [[1, 1.9]]]      # a house of size 1.9 ...
y_out = np.r_[y,   [[0.0]]]         # ... but priced near 0: an outlier
theta_out = np.linalg.inv(X_out.T @ X_out) @ X_out.T @ y_out
print("without outlier:", theta_best.ravel())
print("with outlier   :", theta_out.ravel())   # slope + intercept both shift

3. Break gradient descent on purpose. Set eta = 1.5 and print theta each epoch — watch the numbers explode toward inf/nan. Seeing it diverge beats reading about it.

Solution 
theta = rng.standard_normal((2, 1))
for epoch in range(10):
    theta = theta - 1.5 * (2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y))
    print(epoch, theta.ravel())    # values blow up — the steps overshoot the valley

4. Turn up the noise. Regenerate y with 3× the noise and re-fit — see how far the recovered parameters drift from the true 4 and 3.

Solution 
y_noisy = 4 + 3 * X + rng.standard_normal((m, 1)) * 3
theta_noisy = np.linalg.inv(X_b.T @ X_b) @ X_b.T @ y_noisy
print(theta_noisy.ravel())         # noticeably further from [4, 3]

docs.title: C1 · W2 — Multiple Features, Feature Scaling & Polynomial Regression, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 1 · Week 2 lessons that the code builds on — many features at once, the vectorization trick, why scaling matters, and bending the line into a curve:

  • Multiple Features
  • Vectorization
  • Feature Scaling → Part 2
  • Polynomial Regression

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

Week 1 fit a line through one feature. This week does three things that turn that toy into the workhorse you'll actually use: predict from many features at once (one dot product), scale those features so gradient descent stops crawling, and bend the straight line into a curve by feeding it powers of a feature. We'll build each from scratch in NumPy so you see the math become code, then reach for the scikit-learn one-liner you'd type on the job.

The through-line: everything here is still linear regression. More features, scaled features, and polynomial features are all just different columns handed to the same w · x + b engine from last week.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
We'll predict house price from two features on wildly different scales — square footage (hundreds to thousands) and bedroom count (1–5) — plus noise, from a known formula so we can check our answers.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)              # fixed seed → reproducible "random" data
m = 100                                       # number of training examples

size     = rng.uniform(300, 2000, m)          # feature 1: sq ft — a big range
bedrooms = rng.integers(1, 6, m).astype(float)  # feature 2: 1–5 — a tiny range
X = np.column_stack([size, bedrooms])         # shape (m, 2): one row per house

true_w, true_b = np.array([0.15, 20.0]), 50.0  # the formula we'll try to recover
y = X @ true_w + true_b + rng.standard_normal(m) * 10

X is now m rows × n = 2 columns. In the lesson's notation each row is x⁽ⁱ⁾ (the vector of features for one house) and x⁽ⁱ⁾ⱼ is feature j of example i. The two features spanning very different ranges — 300–2000 vs. 1–5 — is exactly the setup that makes scaling matter later.

docs.title: 1. The model with many features is one dot product
docs.text:
The lesson's multiple-feature model is

\[f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}) = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b.\]

That weighted sum is a dot product. You could compute it three ways — spelled out term by term, in a for loop, or vectorized in one line — and only the last one scales:

w = np.array([0.15, 20.0])
b = 50.0
x = X[0]                                   # one house

term_by_term = w[0]*x[0] + w[1]*x[1] + b   # fine for n=2, hopeless for n=100,000
loop         = sum(w[j]*x[j] for j in range(len(w))) + b
vectorized   = np.dot(w, x) + b            # the one you actually write
print(term_by_term, loop, vectorized)      # all identical

np.dot (or the @ operator) hands the whole sum to NumPy's optimized linear-algebra routines, which use your CPU/GPU's parallel hardware instead of stepping through one term at a time in Python. For the whole dataset at once it's a single matrix multiply:

def predict(X, w, b):
    return X @ w + b        # ŷ for every row, in one shot

print(predict(X, w, b)[:5])   # first five predicted prices

docs.title: See why vectorization wins
docs.text:
Not a style preference — it's a speed cliff. Time the loop against the dot product on a million-element vector:

import time
n = 1_000_000
big_w, big_x = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)

t = time.perf_counter()
s = sum(big_w[j]*big_x[j] for j in range(n))
print(f"python loop: {time.perf_counter()-t:.4f}s")

t = time.perf_counter()
s = np.dot(big_w, big_x)
print(f"np.dot     : {time.perf_counter()-t:.4f}s")   # typically ~100× faster

Same math, two orders of magnitude apart. Every model you train from here on leans on this.

docs.title: 2. Gradient descent for many features, from scratch
docs.text:
Last week's gradient-descent loop already generalizes to n features with almost no change — the gradient formula is identical, it just runs over every column at once. We'll keep the bias b separate from the weights w (that's how the lessons and scikit-learn both do it):

def gradient_descent(X, y, eta, n_epochs):
    m, n = X.shape
    w, b = np.zeros(n), 0.0
    for _ in range(n_epochs):
        err = X @ w + b - y                # residual for every example, shape (m,)
        w  -= eta * (2 / m) * (X.T @ err)  # one gradient step for all n weights
        b  -= eta * (2 / m) * err.sum()    # ... and the bias
    return w, b

Now try to train it on the raw features and watch it fall apart:

w, b = gradient_descent(X, y, eta=1e-2, n_epochs=1000)
print(w, b)        # → nan nan ... : it diverged

nan. The size column (up to 2000) makes its slice of the gradient enormous, so a learning rate the bedroom column can tolerate sends the size weight rocketing off to infinity. You can rescue it by shrinking eta until the biggest feature behaves —

w, b = gradient_descent(X, y, eta=1e-7, n_epochs=100_000)
print(w, b)        # crawls toward the answer, but needs a tiny step + tons of epochs

— but now the step is so small that the bedroom weight barely moves. That's the tall-skinny- contour problem from the lesson: one learning rate can't suit both scales at once. The fix isn't a cleverer eta, it's making the features comparable.

docs.title: 3. Feature scaling from scratch — z-score normalization
docs.text:
The lesson gives three recipes (divide-by-max, mean normalization, z-score). The one the assignments and every library default to is z-score / standardization: subtract each feature's mean, divide by its standard deviation, so every column ends up centered at 0 with spread 1.

\[x'_j = \frac{x_j - \mu_j}{\sigma_j}\]

Done per column, it's four lines of NumPy:

def zscore(X):
    mu    = X.mean(axis=0)      # per-column mean   → shape (n,)
    sigma = X.std(axis=0)       # per-column stddev → shape (n,)
    return (X - mu) / sigma, mu, sigma

X_scaled, mu, sigma = zscore(X)
print(X_scaled.mean(axis=0).round(6), X_scaled.std(axis=0).round(6))  # ≈ [0 0]  [1 1]

Return mu and sigma, not just the scaled matrix — you need the exact same shift and scale to transform any future house before predicting (never re-fit them on new data). Now the identical gradient-descent loop, same eta, converges almost instantly:

w_s, b_s = gradient_descent(X_scaled, y, eta=0.1, n_epochs=1000)
print(w_s, b_s)     # converges fast — no nan, no 100k epochs

One learning rate now suits both weights because both features live on the same scale — the skinny contours became round, and gradient descent walks straight to the bottom. The weights w_s are in scaled space, so to predict a new house you scale it with the stored mu/sigma first:

new_house = np.array([[1500, 3]])                 # 1500 sq ft, 3 bedrooms
pred = ((new_house - mu) / sigma) @ w_s + b_s
print(pred)                                        # price in the same units as y

docs.title: 4. The library way — StandardScaler
docs.text:
In real code you don't hand-roll zscore; scikit-learn's StandardScaler is the exact same math with fit (learn mu/sigma from the training set) and transform (apply them) separated so you can't accidentally leak the test set into your scaling:

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)        # learns + applies mean/std in one call
print(scaler.mean_, scaler.scale_)        # the same mu and sigma you computed by hand

Fit on training data only. Once fitted, call scaler.transform(X_new) on validation, test, or live data — reusing the training mu/sigma, exactly like passing your stored values around above. Géron's warning: never call fit() on anything but the training set.

scikit-learn also ships MinMaxScaler (the divide-to-a-range recipe, default 0–1). Reach for StandardScaler by default — it's far less rattled by outliers, since one bad value can't crush every other value into a sliver the way min-max rescaling can.

docs.title: 5. Polynomial regression from scratch — powers as features
docs.text:
A straight line can't follow curved data. The trick: manufacture new features by raising an existing one to powers, then hand them to the same linear model. That's polynomial regression — still linear in the parameters, just fed nonlinear columns.

Generate curved data from a quadratic, the way Géron does:

m = 200
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, (m, 1))                        # one feature
y = 0.5 * x[:, 0]**2 + x[:, 0] + 2 + rng.standard_normal(m)   # quadratic + noise

Now build the extra column by hand — stack x and x² side by side — and you've turned a one-feature problem into a two-feature one that a plain line can fit:

X_poly = np.column_stack([x[:, 0], x[:, 0]**2])       # features: [x, x²]

Feature scaling is now essential, not optional. If x spans a few units, x² spans its square and higher powers explode further — wildly different scales, the exact thing that broke gradient descent in §2. So scale, then fit (we'll reuse the closed-form normal equation from last week's lab since it needs no learning rate):

X_poly_scaled, mu, sigma = zscore(X_poly)
X_b = np.c_[np.ones((m, 1)), X_poly_scaled]           # prepend the bias column
theta = np.linalg.inv(X_b.T @ X_b) @ X_b.T @ y        # normal equation
print(theta)          # bias, then weights on the (scaled) x and x² columns

The model has recovered the curve — it learned to weight the x² column heavily because the data really was quadratic. Powers aren't the only choice: a √x feature (np.sqrt) fits a shape that rises then flattens without ever turning back down, as the lesson notes.

docs.title: 6. The library way — PolynomialFeatures in a pipeline
docs.text:
scikit-learn generates the power columns for you with PolynomialFeatures, and a pipeline chains "make powers → scale → fit" into one object so you never scale the wrong split or forget a step:

from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = make_pipeline(
    PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False),   # adds x², (and cross-terms if >1 feature)
    StandardScaler(),                                    # scales every generated column
    LinearRegression(),
)
model.fit(x, y)
lin = model.named_steps["linearregression"]
print(lin.intercept_, lin.coef_)     # ≈ the 2, 1, 0.5 that generated the data

fit/predict on the whole pipeline runs all three steps in order — model.predict(x_new) makes the powers, scales them with the training statistics, and applies the weights, all automatically. With multiple input features, PolynomialFeatures(degree=d) also adds every cross-term (x₁x₂, x₁²x₂, …), which plain linear regression can't discover on its own — handy, but the column count blows up fast, so keep degree small.

docs.title: How much curve is too much
docs.text:
More powers always fit the training data better — a high enough degree can thread every point — but that's memorizing noise, not learning the pattern (overfitting, which Week 3 tackles). Géron's tool for spotting it is the learning curve: train on growing slices of data and plot train vs. validation error.

from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve

for degree in (2, 15):
    pipe = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False),
                         StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())
    sizes, train_sc, val_sc = learning_curve(
        pipe, x, y, train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10), cv=5,
        scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
    gap = (-val_sc.mean(axis=1))[-1] - (-train_sc.mean(axis=1))[-1]
    print(f"degree {degree:2d}: train–valid gap = {gap:.2f}")   # degree 15's gap is much wider

A big gap between the curves — great on train, worse on validation — is the fingerprint of overfitting. Degree 2 (the true shape) keeps them close; degree 15 pulls them apart.

docs.title: 7. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code above, to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away. Do at least the first two.

1. Confirm the from-scratch and library scalers agree. Print your zscore mu/sigma against StandardScaler's mean_/scale_ for the original X. Same numbers?

Solution 
mine_mu, mine_sigma = X.mean(axis=0), X.std(axis=0)
sk = StandardScaler().fit(X)
print("mine   :", mine_mu.round(4), mine_sigma.round(4))
print("sklearn:", sk.mean_.round(4), sk.scale_.round(4))   # identical

2. Watch scaling rescue the learning rate. Rerun gradient_descent on raw X and on X_scaled with the same eta=0.1, and print both results.

Solution 
raw    = gradient_descent(X,        y, eta=0.1, n_epochs=1000)
scaled = gradient_descent(X_scaled, y, eta=0.1, n_epochs=1000)
print("raw features   :", raw)      # nan — diverges
print("scaled features:", scaled)   # converges cleanly at the same eta

3. Try mean normalization instead of z-score. Swap the standard deviation for the range (max − min) in a copy of zscore and confirm gradient descent still converges.

Solution 
def mean_norm(X):
    mu  = X.mean(axis=0)
    rng_ = X.max(axis=0) - X.min(axis=0)
    return (X - mu) / rng_, mu, rng_

Xn, _, _ = mean_norm(X)
print(gradient_descent(Xn, y, eta=0.1, n_epochs=1000))   # also converges

4. Crank up the polynomial degree. Refit the §6 pipeline at degree=1 and degree=10 and compare the training RMSE — see the high-degree model fit the training data tighter.

Solution 
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
for d in (1, 10):
    p = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(d, include_bias=False),
                      StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(x, y)
    print(f"degree {d:2d}: train RMSE = {root_mean_squared_error(y, p.predict(x)):.3f}")
# degree 1 underfits (high RMSE); degree 10 fits training tighter — but risks overfitting

docs.text:

docs.title: C1 · W3 — Logistic Regression, Decision Boundaries & Regularization, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 1 · Week 3 lessons the code builds on — the model, the boundary, the cost, and how regularization tames it:

  • Logistic Regression
  • Decision Boundary
  • Cost Function for Logistic Regression
  • Cost Function with Regularization → Regularized Logistic Regression

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

In Week 1 you fit a straight line to predict a number. Now the target is a label — spam / not-spam, malignant / benign, pass / fail. The trick is small and reuses almost everything you already have: take the same linear score w·x + b, squash it through an S-shaped sigmoid so it lands between 0 and 1, and read that as a probability. The same gradient-descent engine trains it; the only genuinely new pieces are the squashing function, the log loss that replaces squared error, and a regularization knob that stops a flexible model from memorizing its training data.

We'll build it from the inside out:

  1. From scratch in NumPy — sigmoid → probability → log-loss cost → gradient descent, and the decision boundary you can actually plot.
  2. Bend the boundary — polynomial features let logistic regression draw curves, which also lets it overfit — so we add the λ penalty and watch the boundary calm down.
  3. The library way — scikit-learn's LogisticRegression in three lines, where regularization is always on and controlled by C.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
Two features, two classes. We draw two Gaussian blobs — one per class — so a straight line can separate most of them. Each row of X is one example; y is its label (0 or 1).

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)          # fixed seed → reproducible "random" data
m = 200                                   # number of training examples

X0 = rng.normal(loc=[-1.0, -1.0], scale=1.0, size=(m // 2, 2))   # the y=0 cloud
X1 = rng.normal(loc=[ 1.5,  1.5], scale=1.0, size=(m // 2, 2))   # the y=1 cloud
X  = np.vstack([X0, X1])                                          # (200, 2)
y  = np.r_[np.zeros(m // 2), np.ones(m // 2)].reshape(-1, 1)      # (200, 1): 100 zeros then 100 ones

In the lesson's notation there are m = 200 examples, each a pair (x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾) where y⁽ⁱ⁾ ∈ {0, 1}.

docs.title: 1. The sigmoid, from scratch
docs.text:
The one new building block. The sigmoid (a.k.a. logistic) function maps any real number z into the open interval (0, 1):

\[g(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\]

Written with NumPy it's one line, and because np.exp is element-wise it works on a single number or a whole array at once:

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

print(sigmoid(np.array([-6, 0, 6])))   # → [0.0025, 0.5, 0.9975]

Read off the three anchor points that give it the S-shape: a large negative z maps near 0, z = 0 maps exactly to 0.5, and a large positive z maps near 1. That's the whole reason we use it — it turns an unbounded score into something we can read as a probability.

docs.title: 2. The model: linear score → sigmoid → probability
docs.text:
Logistic regression is just linear regression's z = w·x + b with a sigmoid bolted on the end:

\[f_{\vec{w},b}(\vec{x}) = g(\vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\vec{w}\cdot\vec{x}+b)}}\]

We reuse the Week-1 trick — prepend a column of 1s so the bias b becomes "the weight on a feature that's always 1." Then the whole dataset's scores are one matrix multiply, and one sigmoid turns them into probabilities:

X_b = np.c_[np.ones((m, 1)), X]          # prepend x0 = 1 → shape (200, 3)

def predict_proba(X_b, theta):
    return sigmoid(X_b @ theta)          # ŷ = g(X · θ),  θ = [b, w1, w2]

theta holds all three parameters: theta[0] is the bias b, theta[1:] are the two weights. The output is the model's estimated probability that y = 1 — a tumor scoring 0.7 means "70% chance malignant."

The score z = w·x + b is sometimes called the logit or log-odds — it's the log of the ratio between the two class probabilities. You don't need that for the course, but it's why scikit-learn calls this LogisticRegression.

docs.title: 3. The cost: log loss, from scratch
docs.text:
Squared error was perfect for linear regression, but feeding the sigmoid into it produces a wiggly, non-convex surface full of local minima gradient descent can get stuck in. So logistic regression uses a different per-example loss — one that's near 0 for a confident correct prediction and shoots toward ∞ for a confident wrong one:

\[L\big(f, y\big) = \begin{cases} -\log(f) & \text{if } y = 1,\\ -\log(1 - f) & \text{if } y = 0. \end{cases}\]

Because y is only ever 0 or 1, both cases collapse into one line (one term always zeroes out), and the cost is the average over all m examples:

\[J(\vec{w}, b) = -\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Big[y^{(i)}\log\big(f^{(i)}\big) + \big(1 - y^{(i)}\big)\log\big(1 - f^{(i)}\big)\Big]\] 
def log_loss(X_b, y, theta):
    p = predict_proba(X_b, theta)
    eps = 1e-9                                    # guard against log(0) when p hits 0 or 1
    return float(-np.mean(y * np.log(p + eps) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p + eps)))

This isn't arbitrary — it falls out of maximum likelihood estimation (asking which parameters make the observed labels most probable), and crucially it's convex again, so gradient descent reliably finds the one global minimum.

docs.title: 4. Train it: gradient descent, from scratch
docs.text:
Here's the payoff for all the Week-1 work: the gradient of the log loss has the exact same shape as linear regression's — prediction minus truth, times the feature, averaged:

\[\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta_j} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big(f^{(i)} - y^{(i)}\big)\,x_j^{(i)}\]

The only difference from Week 1 is that f is now the sigmoid, not the raw linear score. So the training loop is nearly identical to the linear-regression one:

eta = 0.1                                  # learning rate
n_epochs = 5000
theta = np.zeros((3, 1))                    # start from all-zeros (a flat 0.5-everywhere model)

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    p = sigmoid(X_b @ theta)               # current probabilities
    gradients = X_b.T @ (p - y) / m        # same (ŷ − y)·x form as linear regression
    theta = theta - eta * gradients        # step downhill

print("theta:", theta.ravel())
print("cost :", round(log_loss(X_b, y, theta), 4))

There's no normal equation for logistic regression — no one-line closed-form shortcut like Week 1's — so iterating downhill isn't just a way to train it, it's the only way. Good thing the engine already works.

We can check accuracy by thresholding the probabilities at 0.5:

preds = (predict_proba(X_b, theta) >= 0.5).astype(int)
print("accuracy:", float((preds == y).mean()))   # ~0.98 on these two blobs

docs.title: 5. The decision boundary, plotted
docs.text:
The decision boundary is where the model flips its 0-vs-1 call. Chase the 0.5 threshold back through the math: f ≥ 0.5 exactly when the sigmoid's input z ≥ 0, i.e. when

\[\vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b \ge 0.\]

So the boundary is the line w·x + b = 0. With two features, θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂ = 0 rearranges to a straight line we can draw:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], c=y.ravel(), cmap="bwr", edgecolor="k")

xs = np.array([X[:, 0].min(), X[:, 0].max()])
ys = -(theta[0, 0] + theta[1, 0] * xs) / theta[2, 0]    # solve θ₀+θ₁x₁+θ₂x₂=0 for x₂
plt.plot(xs, ys, "k--", label="decision boundary")

plt.xlabel("x1"); plt.ylabel("x2"); plt.legend(); plt.show()

Points on one side of the dashed line predict 1, the other side predict 0 — and with only raw features the boundary is always a straight line. To bend it, we need more features.

docs.title: 6. Bending the boundary — and overfitting
docs.text:
Some data can't be split by a straight line — imagine one class forming a ring around the other. Just like linear regression, we can feed polynomial features (x₁², x₁x₂, x₂², …) into logistic regression, and the boundary in the original 2-D space becomes a curve (a circle, ellipse, or something wigglier).

Let's make a ring-shaped dataset and a helper that expands two features into all monomials up to a given degree:

from sklearn.datasets import make_circles

Xc, yc = make_circles(n_samples=200, noise=0.12, factor=0.4, random_state=42)
yc = yc.reshape(-1, 1)

def map_features(X2, degree):
    """(m, 2) → all monomials x1^a · x2^b with 1 ≤ a+b ≤ degree (no bias column)."""
    x1, x2 = X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1]
    feats = [x1**(i - j) * x2**j for i in range(1, degree + 1) for j in range(i + 1)]
    return np.column_stack(feats)

Now reuse the same gradient-descent loop, just on the mapped features. A degree-6 map gives the model plenty of freedom — enough to trace a very contorted boundary:

def train(Xmap, y, lam=0.0, eta=0.2, n_epochs=20000):
    Xb = np.c_[np.ones((len(Xmap), 1)), Xmap]     # add bias column
    theta = np.zeros((Xb.shape[1], 1))
    for _ in range(n_epochs):
        p = sigmoid(Xb @ theta)
        grad = Xb.T @ (p - y) / len(y)
        reg = (lam / len(y)) * theta               # the λ penalty (added in the next section)
        reg[0] = 0                                 # never regularize the bias
        theta = theta - eta * (grad + reg)
    return theta

degree = 6
theta_overfit = train(map_features(Xc, degree), yc, lam=0.0)   # lam=0 → NO regularization

To see the boundary now that it's a curve, we evaluate the model on a fine grid and let contourf shade the two regions — this is the "decision regions" plot from Raschka, adapted:

def plot_boundary(theta, degree, X2, y):
    x1s = np.linspace(X2[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X2[:, 0].max() + 0.5, 300)
    x2s = np.linspace(X2[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X2[:, 1].max() + 0.5, 300)
    xx1, xx2 = np.meshgrid(x1s, x2s)
    grid = np.c_[xx1.ravel(), xx2.ravel()]
    G = np.c_[np.ones((len(grid), 1)), map_features(grid, degree)]
    probs = sigmoid(G @ theta).reshape(xx1.shape)
    plt.contourf(xx1, xx2, probs, levels=[0, 0.5, 1], alpha=0.3, cmap="bwr")
    plt.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], c=y.ravel(), cmap="bwr", edgecolor="k")
    plt.show()

plot_boundary(theta_overfit, degree, Xc, yc)

With no penalty and 27 polynomial features, the boundary bends itself into knots to chase every noisy point — a textbook overfit. It nails the training data but would generalize badly. Time for the knob that fixes it.

docs.title: 7. Regularization, from scratch
docs.text:
The cure is to penalize large weights so the model can't contort so freely. Add a term that grows with the size of the weights to the cost:

\[J(\vec{w},b) = \underbrace{-\frac{1}{m}\sum_i\big[\dots\big]}_{\text{fit the data}} \;+\; \frac{\lambda}{2m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j^2.\]

The two terms pull against each other: the first wants to fit every point, the second wants small (simple) weights. λ sets the trade-off, and by convention the bias b is not penalized. In the gradient this adds exactly one term, (λ/m)·wⱼ, to each weight's slope — which is the reg line already in our train function above. So regularizing is just passing a non-zero lam:

theta_reg = train(map_features(Xc, degree), yc, lam=1.0)   # same model, now with λ = 1
plot_boundary(theta_reg, degree, Xc, yc)

Same 27 features, same loop — but the boundary is now a smooth near-circle instead of a tangle. That's regularization doing its job: keeping every feature available while stopping any one weight from dominating. Watch the extremes:

  • λ = 0 → no penalty → the wiggly overfit from §6.
  • λ enormous → all weights driven toward 0 → the model collapses toward a flat constant → underfit.
  • λ just right → keeps the features, fits a sensible smooth boundary.
for lam in (0.0, 1.0, 1000.0):
    th = train(map_features(Xc, degree), yc, lam=lam)
    p = sigmoid(np.c_[np.ones((len(Xc), 1)), map_features(Xc, degree)] @ th)
    acc = float(((p >= 0.5).astype(int) == yc).mean())
    print(f"lambda={lam:>7}:  train accuracy={acc:.3f},  ||w||={np.linalg.norm(th[1:]):.2f}")

Notice how ||w|| (the total weight size) shrinks as λ grows — that's literally what the penalty rewards.

docs.title: 8. The library way — scikit-learn
docs.text:
In real work you don't hand-roll any of this. scikit-learn's LogisticRegression fits the model with a fast, robust convex optimizer (lbfgs by default) and keeps the bias (intercept_) separate from the weights (coef_), so you pass raw X — no bias column:

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

clf = LogisticRegression()
clf.fit(X, y.ravel())                          # sklearn wants a 1-D y

print("bias   :", clf.intercept_)              # ≈ our theta[0]
print("weights:", clf.coef_)                   # ≈ our theta[1:]
print("probs  :", clf.predict_proba(X[:3]))    # P(y=0), P(y=1) per row — they sum to 1
print("labels :", clf.predict(X[:3]))          # the 0/1 call at the 0.5 threshold

One gotcha worth memorizing: scikit-learn's regularization dial is C, not λ, and it's the inverse — C = 1/λ. So a small C means strong regularization (heavy penalty, simpler model) and a large C means weak regularization. And unlike our from-scratch model, sklearn's LogisticRegression regularizes by default (L2). You can watch C do the same thing our λ did — on the ring data, via a polynomial pipeline:

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures

for C in (0.001, 1.0, 1000.0):                 # small C = strong reg = simpler boundary
    model = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(6), LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=10000))
    model.fit(Xc, yc.ravel())
    print(f"C={C:>7}:  train accuracy={model.score(Xc, yc.ravel()):.3f}")

For more than two classes, LogisticRegression generalizes on its own via softmax regression (a.k.a. multinomial logistic regression): instead of one probability it outputs one per class, all summing to 1, and predicts the biggest. Same idea, more outputs — no extra code from you.

docs.title: 9. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code you already ran above, meant to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away if you get stuck. Do at least the first two.

1. Move the threshold. In §5 we predicted 1 when the probability ≥ 0.5. Raise the bar to 0.8 (only confident positives count) and count how many fewer 1s you predict.

Solution 
p = predict_proba(X_b, theta)
print("threshold 0.5:", int((p >= 0.5).sum()), "positives")
print("threshold 0.8:", int((p >= 0.8).sum()), "positives")   # fewer — the bar is higher

2. Watch a confident-but-wrong prediction blow up the loss. Feed log_loss a point the model is sure about and wrong about, and compare its loss to a correct one.

Solution 
# a y=1 example the model calls 0.99 (right) vs 0.01 (confidently wrong)
Xone = np.array([[1.0, 2.0, 2.0]])            # bias col + a point deep in the y=1 blob
right = log_loss(Xone, np.array([[1.0]]), theta)
wrong = log_loss(Xone, np.array([[0.0]]), theta)   # same point, label flipped to 0
print("loss when right:", round(right, 3))
print("loss when wrong:", round(wrong, 3))    # far larger — confident-wrong is punished hard

3. Turn regularization off and see the overfit. Re-run §7's boundary with lam=0.0 next to lam=1.0 and eyeball how much wigglier the unregularized curve is.

Solution 
plot_boundary(train(map_features(Xc, degree), yc, lam=0.0), degree, Xc, yc)   # tangled
plot_boundary(train(map_features(Xc, degree), yc, lam=1.0), degree, Xc, yc)   # smooth

4. Crank λ to the underfit extreme. Train with lam=1e5 and check the weights nearly vanish, leaving an almost-flat model.

Solution 
th = train(map_features(Xc, degree), yc, lam=1000.0)
print("||w|| =", round(float(np.linalg.norm(th[1:])), 4))   # ≈ 0: weights crushed
plot_boundary(th, degree, Xc, yc)                            # boundary barely bends

5. Confirm from-scratch ≈ scikit-learn. On the linear blob data, print your §4 theta next to sklearn's [intercept_, coef_]. (They won't be identical — sklearn regularizes by default and uses a different optimizer — but the sign and rough size should match.)

Solution 
print("scratch :", theta.ravel())
print("sklearn :", np.r_[clf.intercept_, clf.coef_.ravel()])
# weaken sklearn's regularization (big C) to line them up more closely:
strong = LogisticRegression(C=1e6).fit(X, y.ravel())
print("sklearn (C=1e6):", np.r_[strong.intercept_, strong.coef_.ravel()])

docs.title: C2 · W1 — Neural Networks & Forward Propagation, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 2 · Week 1 lessons that the code builds on — what a layer is, how inference runs, and the vectorized version:

  • Neural Network Layer
  • Inference: Making Predictions (Forward Propagation)
  • Forward Prop in a Single Layer → Matrix Multiplication Code

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

Here's the one idea the whole week rests on: a neuron is just a logistic-regression unit, and a layer is a stack of them. Once you believe that, a neural network is nothing exotic — it's the g(w·x + b) you already know, repeated a few times, with the output of one layer becoming the input to the next. That "run left to right, layer by layer" pass is forward propagation.

We'll build it from the inside out:

  1. One neuron, by hand — the literal z = w·x + b, a = g(z) from the lesson.
  2. A whole layer at once — the same thing vectorized into one matmul, so 3 neurons cost the same code as 1.
  3. Stack the layers — chain two dense calls and you have forward propagation through a real 2→3→1 network.
  4. The library way — PyTorch's nn.Sequential, which is what you'd actually ship.

All four compute the exact same thing. Seeing that is the whole point.

Copy/terminal lab (no in-browser runner)

The PyTorch sections can't run in the browser (Pyodide has no torch). Copy the blocks into a terminal or notebook with pip install torch. The NumPy sections run anywhere.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
We'll reuse the course's coffee-roasting example: two features — roast temperature (°C) and duration (minutes) — and the network predicts whether the beans come out good.

import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))     # g(z), the logistic function from Course 1

x = np.array([200.0, 17.0])             # one example: 200°C for 17 minutes

x is a single training example with 2 features. That's a⁽⁰⁾ in the lesson's notation — the "activation" of layer 0, which is just the raw input.

Two features live on wildly different scales (200 vs 17), which makes the raw dot products huge and saturates the sigmoid. Real networks normalize first, so let's do that — it makes the activations land in an interesting range instead of pinned at 0 or 1:

mu = np.array([200.0, 15.0])            # rough feature means
sd = np.array([15.0, 3.0])             # rough feature spreads
x_norm = (x - mu) / sd                  # → about [0.0, 0.67]

docs.title: 1. One neuron, by hand
docs.text:
Straight from the Forward Prop in a Single Layer lesson: a neuron takes the input vector, dots it with its own weights, adds its bias, and squashes the result through the sigmoid. Here's the first unit of layer 1, with its own w and b:

w1_1 = np.array([ 1.5, -2.0]);  b1_1 = -0.5     # weights + bias for unit 1
z1_1 = np.dot(w1_1, x_norm) + b1_1              # net input:  z = w·x + b
a1_1 = sigmoid(z1_1)                            # activation: a = g(z)
print(a1_1)                                     # a single number in (0, 1)

That's it — that's a neuron. z1_1 is the net input (the same weighted sum from linear regression), and a1_1 is the activation. The notation w1_1 reads as \(\vec{w}^{[1]}_1\): layer 1, unit 1.

A layer of 3 neurons is just this, three times, each with its own parameters. Grouping the three activations into one vector gives the layer's output a⁽¹⁾:

w1_2 = np.array([-3.0,  4.0]);  b1_2 =  0.2
w1_3 = np.array([ 2.0,  1.0]);  b1_3 = -1.0

a1_2 = sigmoid(np.dot(w1_2, x_norm) + b1_2)
a1_3 = sigmoid(np.dot(w1_3, x_norm) + b1_3)

a1 = np.array([a1_1, a1_2, a1_3])               # the layer-1 activation vector
print(a1)                                       # 3 numbers, one per unit

This works, but writing out a line per neuron is exactly the tedium the lesson warns about. A 25-unit layer would be 25 copies. Time to vectorize.

docs.title: 2. A whole layer at once — the vectorized dense
docs.text:
The trick from Matrix Multiplication Code: stack every neuron's weights as the columns of one matrix W, and the whole layer becomes a single matrix multiply plus one bias add. No loop over neurons.

W1 = np.array([[ 1.5, -3.0,  2.0],      # column j = weights of unit j
               [-2.0,  4.0,  1.0]])     # shape: (n_inputs=2, n_units=3)
b1 = np.array([-0.5,  0.2, -1.0])       # one bias per unit, shape (3,)

def dense(a_in, W, b, g=sigmoid):
    z = a_in @ W + b                    # net inputs for ALL units at once
    return g(z)                         # activations for ALL units at once

a1_vec = dense(x_norm, W1, b1)
print(a1_vec)                           # identical to the a1 we built by hand

The W1 I picked has exactly the per-neuron weights from Section 1 as its columns, so a1_vec matches a1 to the last decimal — the vectorized version is the same computation, just written once instead of three times. One dense call handles a 3-unit layer or a 3000-unit layer with no code change, and @ (matrix multiply) is the operation modern GPUs are built to run fast.

A note on the row-vs-column convention

The course slides write \(Z = A^{\top}W + B\) because they picture the input as a column. In code it's cleaner to keep each example as a row — that's the TensorFlow/PyTorch convention — so we write a_in @ W + b with no transpose. Same numbers, one fewer .T. When you batch many examples, a_in becomes a (n_examples, n_inputs) matrix and this exact line still works — every example flows through in parallel.

docs.title: 3. Stack the layers — that's forward propagation
docs.text:
Now the payoff. A network is just layers where each layer's output is the next layer's input. Our 2→3→1 coffee network is one hidden layer (dense above) feeding an output layer with a single unit. Chaining the calls left-to-right is forward propagation:

# Output layer: 1 unit, takes the 3 hidden activations as input
W2 = np.array([[ 3.0],                  # shape (n_inputs=3, n_units=1)
               [-4.0],
               [ 2.0]])
b2 = np.array([0.5])

def forward(x, W1, b1, W2, b2):
    a1 = dense(x,  W1, b1)              # layer 1: 2 features → 3 activations
    a2 = dense(a1, W2, b2)             # layer 2: 3 activations → 1 output
    return a2

y_hat = forward(x_norm, W1, b1, W2, b2)
print(y_hat)                            # a single probability in (0, 1)

That's a complete neural network making a prediction. Read forward top to bottom and you're literally watching the activations propagate forward: x → a¹ → a². For the digit network in the lesson (64 → 25 → 15 → 1) you'd just add more dense lines — nothing else changes.

To turn the probability into a yes/no decision, threshold it at 0.5, exactly like logistic regression:

prediction = int(y_hat[0] >= 0.5)       # 1 = good roast, 0 = bad roast
print(prediction)

Why this is a big deal: we never wrote a training loop. With the weights already set, forward propagation alone runs the network. This is exactly how you'd download someone else's trained weights and run inference on your own data. Learning those weights (back- propagation) is next week — but the prediction machinery is already complete.

docs.title: 4. The library way — PyTorch nn.Sequential
docs.text:
In practice you don't hand-roll dense. A neural network that's "just a stack of layers" maps perfectly onto PyTorch's nn.Sequential, which chains modules: it feeds the input to the first, its output to the second, and so on — forward propagation, done for you.

Ng's lectures use TensorFlow; this lab uses PyTorch

The concepts are identical — a stack of dense layers with activations — only the library names differ. PyTorch is the de-facto industry and research standard today, so we build in it here. Wherever Ng writes tf.keras.Sequential([Dense(3), Dense(1)]), the PyTorch below is the same network.

import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 3),      # hidden layer: 2 inputs → 3 units  (= our dense(x, W1, b1))
    nn.Sigmoid(),         # the activation g applied to layer 1
    nn.Linear(3, 1),      # output layer: 3 inputs → 1 unit
    nn.Sigmoid(),         # activation g applied to the output
)

x_t = torch.tensor([[0.0, 0.67]])       # one example, as a (1, 2) tensor (row = example)
with torch.no_grad():                   # inference only — no gradients needed
    y_hat_torch = model(x_t)
print(y_hat_torch)                       # a (1, 1) tensor: the probability

A few things worth noticing:

  • nn.Linear(2, 3) is our dense — it holds a (3, 2) weight matrix and a (3,) bias, and computes x @ W.T + b when called. PyTorch initializes those weights randomly, so your number won't match Section 3 — it's an untrained network (real weights come from training).
  • The activation is its own module. nn.Linear does only the linear w·x + b; the nn.Sigmoid after it applies g. Stacking them reproduces a = g(w·x + b).
  • model(x_t) is the entire forward pass — the same x → a¹ → a² chain you wrote by hand in Section 3, now one call.
  • Real MLPs usually use nn.ReLU between hidden layers instead of sigmoid (faster to train, more on that next week); sigmoid stays natural on the final layer for a probability.

You can peek at the parameters PyTorch is holding — the shapes line up with our W1/W2:

for name, p in model.named_parameters():
    print(name, tuple(p.shape))
# 0.weight (3, 2)   0.bias (3,)   2.weight (1, 3)   2.bias (1,)

docs.title: 5. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code you already ran above, meant to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away if you get stuck. Do at least the first two.

1. Confirm hand-coded and vectorized agree. Print a1 (from Section 1) and a1_vec (from Section 2) side by side. Are they equal?

Solution 
print("by hand   :", a1)
print("vectorized:", a1_vec)
print("match?", np.allclose(a1, a1_vec))   # → True: same computation

2. Batch several examples through forward. Stack three roasts into a (3, 2) matrix and call forward once — every example flows through in parallel, no loop.

Solution 
X = np.array([[0.0, 0.67],      # each row is one normalized example
              [1.0, -0.5],
              [-0.5, 0.0]])
print(forward(X, W1, b1, W2, b2))   # shape (3, 1): one probability per row

3. Make the network deeper. Add a second hidden layer (3 units) to forward — a 2→3→3→1 network. You'll need a new W_mid of shape (3, 3) and a bias of shape (3,).

Solution 
W_mid = np.array([[ 1.0, -1.0,  0.5],
                  [ 0.5,  2.0, -1.0],
                  [-1.0,  0.5,  1.0]])
b_mid = np.array([0.0, 0.1, -0.2])

def forward_deep(x):
    a1 = dense(x,  W1,    b1)
    a2 = dense(a1, W_mid, b_mid)   # extra layer, same dense()
    a3 = dense(a2, W2,    b2)
    return a3

print(forward_deep(x_norm))        # still one probability out

4. Swap the hidden activation to ReLU in PyTorch. Change the first nn.Sigmoid() to nn.ReLU() and re-run the forward pass. The output still comes out in (0, 1) because the final layer is still a sigmoid.

Solution 
model_relu = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 3),
    nn.ReLU(),              # ← hidden activation changed
    nn.Linear(3, 1),
    nn.Sigmoid(),
)
with torch.no_grad():
    print(model_relu(x_t))  # different number, still a valid probability

docs.title: C2 · W2 — Training Neural Networks: Activations, Softmax & Backprop, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 2 · Week 2 lessons that the code turns into working networks — the activation choices, the softmax output, the optimizer, and the machinery that computes the gradients:

  • Alternatives to the Sigmoid Activation → Choosing Activation Functions
  • Softmax
  • Advanced Optimization
  • Computation Graph

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

The lessons covered four ideas that turn a stack of neurons into something you can actually train: which activation function to use where, the softmax output for multiclass problems, the Adam optimizer, and back-prop — the right-to-left pass that finds every gradient. This lab wires them together from the inside out:

  1. From scratch, in NumPy — build the activations, the softmax, and the cross-entropy loss, then run back-prop by hand on a tiny computation graph so you see exactly what the framework does.
  2. A from-scratch classifier — a one-layer softmax classifier trained with the gradient you derived, so you watch the loop learn.
  3. The library way — PyTorch — the same network in a dozen lines, with Adam and autograd doing the calculus for you. This is what you'd actually type on the job.

A note on the framework: Ng's lectures use TensorFlow/Keras, but this lab uses PyTorch — it's the de-facto industry standard for research and most new production work. The concepts are identical: a Dense layer is an nn.Linear, SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True) is nn.CrossEntropyLoss, and Adam is Adam. Only the spelling changes.

docs.title: 0. Setup
docs.text:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)     # fixed seed → reproducible "random" numbers

We'll bring in scikit-learn and PyTorch as we reach those sections.

docs.title: 1. The activation zoo, from scratch
docs.text:
An activation function g(z) is the little non-linear kink applied to each neuron's weighted sum z = w·x + b. The three the lesson names are one line each:

def linear(z):   return z                    # "no activation" — g(z) = z
def sigmoid(z):  return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))  # squashes to (0, 1)
def relu(z):     return np.maximum(0, z)      # max(0, z) — flat below 0, 45° line above

z = np.array([-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0])
print("linear :", linear(z))    # [-3. -1.  0.  1.  3.]
print("sigmoid:", sigmoid(z).round(3))   # [0.047 0.269 0.5   0.731 0.953]
print("relu   :", relu(z))      # [0. 0. 0. 1. 3.]

Read off the ranges from the lesson: linear is unbounded (−∞, ∞), sigmoid is capped at (0, 1), ReLU is [0, ∞) — flat 0 for negative inputs, then it just passes the input through. That last property is why ReLU became the default hidden-layer choice: it's dirt cheap (no exponential), and unlike sigmoid it's flat on only one side, so gradient descent doesn't stall on a plateau.

docs.title: Why we need the non-linearity at all
docs.text:
Here's the argument Géron makes, in code. Stack two linear layers and you get… one linear layer. The kink is the whole point.

W1 = rng.standard_normal((3, 4))     # layer 1: 3 inputs → 4 units
W2 = rng.standard_normal((4, 2))     # layer 2: 4 units  → 2 outputs
x  = rng.standard_normal(3)

two_linear_layers = (x @ W1) @ W2        # no activation between them
one_equivalent    = x @ (W1 @ W2)        # ... collapses to a single matrix
print(np.allclose(two_linear_layers, one_equivalent))   # True

Two linear layers are exactly one linear layer (W1 @ W2 is just another matrix). No matter how many you stack, without a non-linearity in between the whole network can only draw a straight line. Slotting a ReLU (or sigmoid) between the layers is what lets a deep net bend into complex shapes.

docs.title: 2. Choosing an activation — match the output to the label
docs.text:
Hidden layers are easy: use ReLU. The interesting choice is the output layer, and it's driven entirely by what your target y can be (straight from the lesson):

If y is… Output activation Why 0 or 1 (binary) sigmoid output = P(y=1) any value, ± (e.g. price change) linear g(z) can be negative ≥ 0 only (e.g. a house price) ReLU never negative one of K classes (multiclass) softmax a probability per class, summing to 1

That last row is this week's new tool. Let's build it.

docs.title: 3. Softmax, from scratch
docs.text:
Softmax generalises the sigmoid from two classes to K. Compute one score zⱼ per class, then exponentiate-and-normalise so the outputs are positive and sum to 1:

\[a_j = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} e^{z_k}} = P(y = j \mid x)\]

The naive translation is one line:

def softmax_naive(z):
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

print(softmax_naive(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])).round(3))   # [0.09 0.245 0.665]  → sums to 1

docs.title: The numerical-stability fix
docs.text:
The lesson on the improved softmax warned that e^{zⱼ} blows up for large z — and that's not hypothetical:

print(softmax_naive(np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])))   # [nan nan nan] — exp() overflowed

The fix is a one-line identity: subtracting a constant from every score leaves the softmax unchanged (the constant cancels top and bottom), so subtract the max to force the largest exponent to e^0 = 1:

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)    # shift so the biggest logit is 0 — same result, no overflow
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

print(softmax(np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])).round(3))   # [0.09 0.245 0.665] — identical, no nan

The axis=-1, keepdims=True makes this work row-wise on a whole batch of logits at once. This is the version to use — same math, no overflow. It's exactly why frameworks fold the softmax into the loss (from_logits=True in Keras, CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch): they rearrange the terms internally to dodge those extremes.

docs.title: 4. The cross-entropy loss, from scratch
docs.text:
Softmax gives probabilities; the loss says how good they are. For the true class j, the cross-entropy loss is just −log aⱼ — small when the model is confident and right, large when it's confident and wrong:

def cross_entropy(probs, y):
    m = len(y)
    correct = probs[np.arange(m), y]        # pick each row's true-class probability
    return -np.mean(np.log(correct + 1e-12))   # +tiny to avoid log(0)

probs = np.array([[0.7, 0.2, 0.1],   # example 0, true class 0 → confident & right → low loss
                  [0.1, 0.2, 0.7]])  # example 1, true class 0 → confident & wrong → high loss
print(cross_entropy(probs, y=np.array([0, 0])).round(3))   # 1.328

The curve −log a is near 0 when a → 1 and shoots up as a → 0, so minimising it pushes the probability of the correct class toward 1.

docs.title: 5. Back-prop by hand — the computation graph
docs.text:
Now the heart of it. Back-prop is how frameworks get the gradients — and it's nothing more than the chain rule applied right-to-left across a computation graph. Let's do the lesson's exact tiny example by hand, then check it.

One linear unit a = wx + b with squared-error cost J = ½(a − y)², on a single example x = −2, y = 2, starting at w = 2, b = 8.

Forward pass (left → right) — break it into named intermediate nodes:

x, y, w, b = -2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 8.0

c = w * x          # -4
a = c + b          #  4
d = a - y          #  2
J = 0.5 * d**2     #  2.0
print(c, a, d, J)  # -4.0 4.0 2.0 2.0

Backward pass (right → left) — at each node ask "if I nudge this up by ε, how much does J move?" Each answer is the previous answer times the local derivative (the chain rule):

dJ_dd = d                # J = ½d²  → dJ/dd = d = 2
dJ_da = dJ_dd * 1        # d = a - y → local slope 1
dJ_dc = dJ_da * 1        # a = c + b → local slope 1  (b passes straight through too)
dJ_db = dJ_da * 1        # a = c + b → dJ/db = 2
dJ_dw = dJ_dc * x        # c = w·x   → local slope x = -2

print("dJ/dw =", dJ_dw)  # -4.0
print("dJ/db =", dJ_db)  #  2.0

That dJ/dw = −4 matches the lesson exactly. Notice the efficiency the lesson emphasised: dJ_da was computed once and reused for both dJ/dw and dJ/db. Going right-to-left, every shared sub-result is computed a single time — that's why back-prop scales to millions of parameters.

docs.title: Gradient check — prove it's right
docs.text:
Don't trust hand-derived gradients; check them against the definition of a derivative (nudge w by a tiny ε and re-measure J):

def J_of_w(w_):
    return 0.5 * (w_ * x + b - y) ** 2

eps = 1e-6
numeric = (J_of_w(w + eps) - J_of_w(w - eps)) / (2 * eps)
print(numeric)     # ≈ -4.0 — matches dJ_dw

If the numeric and analytic gradients agree, your back-prop is correct. This is the single most useful debugging trick you'll learn this course.

docs.title: 6. A softmax classifier, trained from scratch
docs.text:
Chain sections 3–5 together and you have a trainable model. For a one-layer softmax classifier, the forward pass is logits → softmax → cross-entropy, and the whole back-prop collapses to one beautiful line: the gradient of cross-entropy-with-softmax with respect to the logits is just (predicted probs − one-hot truth). No messy exp's survive — they cancel.

from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

X, y = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=3, n_features=2, random_state=42)
X = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)          # standardize features
m, n = X.shape
K = 3
Y = np.eye(K)[y]                        # one-hot targets, shape (m, K)

W = rng.standard_normal((n, K)) * 0.01  # weights, one column per class
b = np.zeros(K)

eta = 0.5
for epoch in range(500):
    logits = X @ W + b                  # (m, K)
    probs  = softmax(logits)            # our stable softmax from §3
    loss   = -np.mean(np.sum(Y * np.log(probs + 1e-12), axis=1))

    dlogits = (probs - Y) / m           # ← the whole gradient, in one line
    dW = X.T @ dlogits                  # (n, K)
    db = dlogits.sum(axis=0)            # (K,)

    W -= eta * dW                       # gradient-descent step
    b -= eta * db

acc = (softmax(X @ W + b).argmax(1) == y).mean()
print(f"final loss {loss:.3f}, train accuracy {acc:.1%}")   # near-zero loss, ~100% (blobs separate cleanly)

That's a complete neural-network training loop in ten lines — forward pass, loss, back-prop, update — no framework. The (probs - Y) gradient is the same object PyTorch's autograd computes for you in the next section; you've just done it by hand once so you know it's not magic.

docs.title: 7. The library way — PyTorch
docs.text:
In real work you don't hand-derive gradients — you declare the network and let autograd run back-prop, and let Adam adapt the step size per parameter. Here's the same multiclass job on the Iris dataset (3 flower species), the way you'd actually write it.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

iris = load_iris()
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(iris.data, iris.target, test_size=0.33, random_state=1)

mu, sd = Xtr.mean(0), Xtr.std(0)                          # standardize with TRAIN stats only
Xtr = torch.tensor((Xtr - mu) / sd, dtype=torch.float32)
Xte = torch.tensor((Xte - mu) / sd, dtype=torch.float32)
ytr = torch.tensor(ytr)                                   # int64 class indices
yte = torch.tensor(yte)

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(4, 16), nn.ReLU(),      # hidden layers: ReLU (the default from the lesson)
    nn.Linear(16, 16), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(16, 3),                 # output: 3 raw logits — NO softmax here (see below)
)

loss_fn   = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()                          # folds softmax IN — the from_logits trick
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)  # Adam: the de-facto default optimizer

for epoch in range(200):
    logits = model(Xtr)               # forward pass
    loss   = loss_fn(logits, ytr)     # softmax + cross-entropy, numerically stable
    optimizer.zero_grad()             # clear last step's gradients
    loss.backward()                   # back-prop — autograd fills in every gradient
    optimizer.step()                  # Adam updates every parameter

with torch.no_grad():
    acc = (model(Xte).argmax(1) == yte).float().mean()
print(f"test accuracy {acc:.1%}")     # ~96%

Three things map straight back to the lessons:

  • ReLU on the hidden layers, nothing on the output. The final nn.Linear emits raw logits, not probabilities — deliberately.
  • CrossEntropyLoss expects logits. It applies log-softmax inside the loss — exactly the numerically-stable from_logits=True recipe from the improved-softmax lesson. Putting your own nn.Softmax before it would apply softmax twice (a bug — see Your Turn #4). To read actual probabilities at predict time, run the logits through torch.softmax(logits, dim=1) yourself.
  • Adam replaces plain gradient descent. It keeps a separate, self-adjusting learning rate per parameter — speeding up parameters that move steadily, calming ones that oscillate — which is why it trains faster and is the safe default.

The four-line loop (zero_grad → backward → step) is the PyTorch training loop; you'll write it, essentially unchanged, for every model from here on. loss.backward() is running the exact right-to-left computation-graph pass you did by hand in §5 — just automatically, over thousands of parameters.

docs.title: 8. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code above, meant to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away. Do at least the first two.

1. Sigmoid hidden layers instead of ReLU. Swap both nn.ReLU() for nn.Sigmoid() in the PyTorch model and retrain. Does it still learn? (On this tiny net it works, but watch the loss fall more slowly — the reason the field moved to ReLU.)

Solution 
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(4, 16), nn.Sigmoid(),
    nn.Linear(16, 16), nn.Sigmoid(),
    nn.Linear(16, 3),
)
# re-run the same optimizer + training loop; converges, but typically needs
# more epochs to reach the same accuracy ReLU hit — sigmoid's flat tails slow it down.

2. Break the naive softmax, then fix it. Feed softmax_naive a vector with a large value (e.g. [500., 501., 502.]) and watch it return nan; then confirm the stable softmax handles the same input.

Solution 
big = np.array([500., 501., 502.])
print(softmax_naive(big))   # [nan nan nan] — exp(500) overflows to inf
print(softmax(big).round(3))   # [0.09 0.245 0.665] — the max-subtraction saves it

3. Adam vs. plain SGD. Swap the optimizer for torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01) and retrain. Compare how far the loss has fallen after the same 200 epochs.

Solution 
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)
# ... same training loop ...
# SGD with the same lr usually lands at a higher loss / lower accuracy in 200 epochs —
# Adam's per-parameter adaptive step gets there faster. Bumping SGD's lr helps, but you'd
# have to tune it; Adam is more forgiving out of the box.

4. The double-softmax bug. Add nn.Softmax(dim=1) as the final layer and keep CrossEntropyLoss. Retrain and watch accuracy sag — you've now applied softmax twice.

Solution 
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(4, 16), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(16, 16), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(16, 3), nn.Softmax(dim=1),   # BUG: CrossEntropyLoss softmaxes again
)
# accuracy drops — CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits, not probabilities.
# Lesson: pick ONE place for the softmax; with CrossEntropyLoss it lives inside the loss.

5. Gradient-check the from-scratch classifier. Pick one weight in §6's W, nudge it by ±1e-5, recompute the loss both ways, and confirm the numeric gradient matches that entry of dW.

Solution 
def loss_at(W_):
    p = softmax(X @ W_ + b)
    return -np.mean(np.sum(Y * np.log(p + 1e-12), axis=1))

eps = 1e-5
Wp, Wm = W.copy(), W.copy()
Wp[0, 0] += eps; Wm[0, 0] -= eps
numeric = (loss_at(Wp) - loss_at(Wm)) / (2 * eps)
print(numeric, dW[0, 0])   # ≈ equal — the analytic (probs - Y) gradient is correct
