docs.title: C2 · W3 — Diagnosing Bias & Variance, Learning Curves & Metrics, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 2 · Week 3 lessons it builds on — how to evaluate a model, split the data, read bias vs. variance, and score a skewed classifier:

  • Evaluating a Model
  • Model Selection: Train / CV / Test Sets
  • Diagnosing Bias and Variance → Learning Curves
  • Error Metrics for Skewed Datasets → Trading Off Precision and Recall

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

A model almost never works the first time. This whole week is about the diagnostics that tell you what to try next instead of guessing — and every one of them is just a few numbers you compute from held-out data. In this lab we'll build them from the inside out:

  1. Split the data three ways, then measure error on each — by hand.
  2. Choose a model (which polynomial degree) by its cross-validation error, and read bias vs. variance straight off J_train and J_cv.
  3. Plot learning curves from scratch to decide whether more data would even help.
  4. The library way — scikit-learn's learning_curve, validation_curve, cross_val_score.
  5. Metrics for skewed data — build the confusion matrix, precision, recall, and F1 by hand, then slide the precision/recall trade-off with the decision threshold.

Pure NumPy + scikit-learn throughout.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
We'll generate data from a known quadratic — y = 0.5·x² + x + 2 — plus noise. Because we know the true shape is degree 2, we can watch our diagnostics correctly flag a straight line as too simple and a degree-12 monster as too complex.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = 200
X = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(m, 1))                       # one feature, in [-3, 3]
y = 0.5 * X[:, 0]**2 + X[:, 0] + 2 + rng.standard_normal(m)   # quadratic + noise

X is a column of 200 inputs; y is the noisy target. The standard_normal(m) term is the irreducible error — noise no model can ever fit away.

docs.title: 1. Split it three ways, from scratch
docs.text:
The lesson's fix for "the test set got contaminated" is a three-way split: train (~60%) to fit parameters, cross-validation (~20%) to choose between models, and test (~20%) touched only once at the very end to report the honest generalization number. Shuffle first so each split is a fair sample:

idx = rng.permutation(m)                                  # shuffle the row indices
n_train, n_cv = int(0.6 * m), int(0.2 * m)
tr = idx[:n_train]                                        # 60% → training
cv = idx[n_train:n_train + n_cv]                          # 20% → cross-validation
te = idx[n_train + n_cv:]                                 # 20% → test

X_train, y_train = X[tr], y[tr]
X_cv,    y_cv    = X[cv], y[cv]
X_test,  y_test  = X[te], y[te]
print(len(X_train), len(X_cv), len(X_test))               # → 120 40 40

That's the entire idea. The cross-validation set is the one you're allowed to peek at while tuning; the test set is sealed until you've committed to a model.

docs.title: 2. A cost you can read off any model
docs.text:
To compare models we need one number per dataset: the cost. We'll use Ng's half-mean- squared-error, evaluated without any regularization term (exactly as J_train, J_cv, J_test are defined in the lesson):

def J(model, X, y):
    err = model.predict(X) - y            # residual for each example
    return float(err @ err / (2 * len(y)))    # (1 / 2m) · Σ (f(x) − y)²

We just need something with a .predict(). Here's a from-scratch polynomial regressor: it expands x into x, x², …, x^d, standardizes those columns (high powers explode in magnitude otherwise), and solves the normal equation with pinv for stability:

class PolyReg:
    def __init__(self, degree):
        self.degree = degree

    def _features(self, X):
        return np.hstack([X**p for p in range(1, self.degree + 1)])   # [x, x², …, x^d]

    def fit(self, X, y):
        Z = self._features(X)
        self.mu, self.sd = Z.mean(0), Z.std(0) + 1e-12                # column stats
        Zb = np.c_[np.ones(len(Z)), (Z - self.mu) / self.sd]         # standardize + bias col
        self.theta = np.linalg.pinv(Zb.T @ Zb) @ Zb.T @ y            # normal equation
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        Z = (self._features(X) - self.mu) / self.sd                  # reuse TRAIN stats
        return np.c_[np.ones(len(Z)), Z] @ self.theta

The one subtlety worth noticing: predict reuses the mean and std learned during fit. You standardize the CV and test data with the training statistics — never re-fit the scaler on data you're evaluating, or you've leaked information.

docs.title: 3. Model selection by cross-validation error
docs.text:
Now the core loop from the Model Selection lesson. Fit each candidate degree d on the training set, then score it on the CV set. Pick the d with the lowest J_cv — and crucially, do not pick it by J_test (that would make J_test an optimistic, cheating estimate):

for d in range(1, 11):
    model = PolyReg(d).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"d={d:2d}   J_train={J(model, X_train, y_train):.3f}   J_cv={J(model, X_cv, y_cv):.3f}")

d= 1   J_train=1.395   J_cv=1.340
d= 2   J_train=0.454   J_cv=0.622
d= 3   J_train=0.452   J_cv=0.612
d= 4   J_train=0.451   J_cv=0.609
d= 5   J_train=0.448   J_cv=0.594
...
d=10   J_train=0.435   J_cv=0.635

Look at the two columns. J_train keeps falling as the model gets more flexible — a more complex model can always hug the training points tighter. But J_cv forms a U: high on the left (degree 1 underfits), bottoming out in the low-degree middle, then creeping back up. That U is the whole game. Pick its minimum, then — and only then — unseal the test set:

best_d = min(range(1, 11), key=lambda d: J(PolyReg(d).fit(X_train, y_train), X_cv, y_cv))
final = PolyReg(best_d).fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"chosen degree = {best_d}")
print(f"J_test = {J(final, X_test, y_test):.3f}   (the honest generalization estimate)")

The test number is fair precisely because the test set played no part in choosing best_d.

docs.title: 4. Diagnosing bias vs. variance — the decision rule
docs.text:
The lesson boils diagnosis down to two comparisons. Let's see all three regimes as raw numbers:

for d, X_t, y_t in [(1,  X_train,      y_train),        # underfit: too simple
                    (2,  X_train,      y_train),        # just right
                    (12, X_train[:15], y_train[:15])]:  # overfit: complex model, few points
    model = PolyReg(d).fit(X_t, y_t)
    print(f"d={d:2d}  J_train={J(model, X_t, y_t):8.3f}   J_cv={J(model, X_cv, y_cv):10.3f}")

d= 1  J_train=   1.395   J_cv=     1.340     ← high bias
d= 2  J_train=   0.454   J_cv=     0.622     ← just right
d=12  J_train=   0.140   J_cv= 39325.393     ← high variance

Read it exactly like the slide:

  • High bias (underfit) — J_train is high and J_cv is high and close to it. The model can't even fit the data it trained on. (Degree 1: both ≈ 1.4.)
  • High variance (overfit) — J_cv ≫ J_train. It aced the training points and flunked everything else. (Degree 12 on 15 points: J_train ≈ 0.14, J_cv wildly higher — that absurd number is a degree-12 curve extrapolating between sparse points.)
  • Just right — both low. (Degree 2, the true shape.)

Two comparisons, and you know which direction to move: high bias → a bigger model / more features; high variance → simpler model, more regularization, or more data (next section tells you whether that last one will pay off).

docs.title: 5. Learning curves, from scratch
docs.text:
A learning curve plots error against training-set size m_train. It answers the month-saving question: would collecting more data actually help? Build it by fitting on growing prefixes of the training set and scoring each on the fixed CV set.

High-bias model (a straight line on quadratic data):

for n in (10, 30, 60, 120):
    model = PolyReg(1).fit(X_train[:n], y_train[:n])
    print(f"n={n:3d}   J_train={J(model, X_train[:n], y_train[:n]):.3f}   J_cv={J(model, X_cv, y_cv):.3f}")

n= 10   J_train=0.752   J_cv=1.902
n= 30   J_train=1.350   J_cv=1.677
n= 60   J_train=1.397   J_cv=1.499
n=120   J_train=1.395   J_cv=1.340

J_train rises (a line fits 10 points more easily than 120), J_cv falls, and they converge and plateau — both stuck around 1.4, far above the ~0.5 a good model reaches. Consequence: more data won't help. The curves have already flattened; the gap is bias, not data starvation. You need a better model, not a bigger dataset.

High-variance model (degree 12):

for n in (15, 30, 60, 120):
    model = PolyReg(12).fit(X_train[:n], y_train[:n])
    print(f"n={n:3d}   J_train={J(model, X_train[:n], y_train[:n]):.3f}   J_cv={J(model, X_cv, y_cv):.3f}")

n= 15   J_train=0.140   J_cv=39325.393
n= 30   J_train=0.244   J_cv=0.769
n= 60   J_train=0.348   J_cv=0.748
n=120   J_train=0.424   J_cv=0.629

Now there's a big gap: low J_train, much higher J_cv. But watch the gap shrink as n grows — J_cv marches down toward J_train. Here more data does help. That's the tell: a high-variance gap that keeps closing means "keep collecting examples."

docs.title: 6. The library way — scikit-learn
docs.text:
You don't hand-roll splits and curves on the job. train_test_split carves off a test set; cross_val_score runs k-fold cross-validation (every point serves as validation once — sturdier than one fixed split); learning_curve and validation_curve produce the exact plots above in one call.

from sklearn.model_selection import (train_test_split, cross_val_score,
                                     learning_curve, validation_curve)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

# a degree-d polynomial regressor, standardized, as one object
def poly_model(degree):
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                         PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False),
                         LinearRegression())

k-fold cross-validation — a more robust J_cv than a single split (note the sign: sklearn maximizes a score, so MSE is returned negated):

scores = cross_val_score(poly_model(2), X, y, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
print("per-fold MSE:", np.round(-scores, 3), "  mean:", round(-scores.mean(), 3))

Validation curve — the U from Section 3, automated. Sweep the degree, get train and CV error for each:

degrees = [1, 2, 4, 8, 12]
train_s, valid_s = validation_curve(
    poly_model(1), X, y,
    param_name="polynomialfeatures__degree", param_range=degrees,
    cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
print("degree      :", degrees)
print("train MSE   :", np.round(-train_s.mean(1), 3))   # → [2.943 1.037 1.020 1.003 0.985]
print("valid MSE   :", np.round(-valid_s.mean(1), 3))   # → [2.978 1.066 1.055 1.074 1.136]

Valid MSE dips at degree 2 and creeps up by degree 12 — the same "pick the bottom of the U" story, no loop written.

Learning curve — the Section 5 plot, automated. It retrains on growing subsets and cross-validates each size:

sizes, train_s, valid_s = learning_curve(
    poly_model(2), X, y,
    train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 6), cv=5,
    scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
print("sizes    :", sizes)
print("train MSE:", np.round(-train_s.mean(1), 3))
print("valid MSE:", np.round(-valid_s.mean(1), 3))

To see it, plot both means against sizes (plt.plot(sizes, -train_s.mean(1)) and the same for valid) — converging-and-plateaued means bias, a wide-but-closing gap means variance.

docs.title: 7. Skewed data: when accuracy lies
docs.text:
Switch to classification. When one class is rare, accuracy becomes worthless: the lesson's rare-disease example shows a do-nothing print("y=0") scoring 99.5%. Let's reproduce that trap with a heavily imbalanced dataset (~5% positives):

from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

Xc, yc = make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=10, n_informative=6,
                             n_redundant=0, weights=[0.95, 0.05],
                             class_sep=1.0, random_state=1)
print("positive fraction:", round(yc.mean(), 4))                 # → 0.054

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.3,
                                      stratify=yc, random_state=1)   # keep the ratio in both
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
yhat = clf.predict(Xte)

model_acc  = (yhat == yte).mean()
always_neg = (yte == 0).mean()                                   # the "print y=0" cheat
print(f"model accuracy  = {model_acc:.4f}")                      # → 0.9747
print(f"always-negative = {always_neg:.4f}")                     # → 0.9460

A 97.5% model that barely beats a program that never predicts the disease. Accuracy can't tell them apart — so build the confusion matrix for the rare class y=1, by hand:

tp = int(np.sum((yhat == 1) & (yte == 1)))   # said 1, was 1
fp = int(np.sum((yhat == 1) & (yte == 0)))   # said 1, was 0  (false alarm)
fn = int(np.sum((yhat == 0) & (yte == 1)))   # said 0, was 1  (missed it)
tn = int(np.sum((yhat == 0) & (yte == 0)))   # said 0, was 0
print(f"TP={tp}  FP={fp}  FN={fn}  TN={tn}")                     # → TP=46 FP=3 FN=35 TN=1416

Precision (when it cries "disease", how often is it right?) and recall (of the real cases, how many did it catch?) — the two numbers accuracy was hiding:

precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall    = tp / (tp + fn)
f1        = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)   # harmonic mean
print(f"precision = {precision:.3f}   recall = {recall:.3f}   F1 = {f1:.3f}")
# → precision = 0.939   recall = 0.568   F1 = 0.708

There's the real story: when the model says "positive" it's right 94% of the time, but it only finds 57% of the actual positives. The print("y=0") cheat would have zero TP, so its recall is 0 and F1 is 0 — instantly exposed. F1 is the harmonic mean, which (unlike a plain average) stays low unless both precision and recall are high. scikit-learn agrees:

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

print(confusion_matrix(yte, yhat))                               # [[1416 3] [35 46]]  (rows=actual)
print(precision_score(yte, yhat), recall_score(yte, yhat), f1_score(yte, yhat))

Note sklearn's confusion_matrix lays rows out as actual classes and columns as predicted (the transpose of the lesson's slide) — same four counts, different corner.

docs.title: 8. Trading off precision and recall
docs.text:
Logistic regression outputs a probability; the default rule predicts 1 when it's ≥ 0.5. That 0.5 is a knob. Raise it and you only flag the confident cases (↑ precision, ↓ recall); lower it and you flag anything suspicious (↑ recall, ↓ precision). Sweep it by hand using predict_proba:

proba = clf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]                     # P(y=1) for each test example
for t in (0.3, 0.5, 0.7):
    pred = (proba >= t).astype(int)
    p = precision_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0)
    r = recall_score(yte, pred)
    print(f"threshold={t}:   precision={p:.3f}   recall={r:.3f}")

threshold=0.3:   precision=0.855   recall=0.654     ← catch more, cry wolf more
threshold=0.5:   precision=0.939   recall=0.568
threshold=0.7:   precision=1.000   recall=0.481     ← only the sure things

That's the trade-off in three lines: as the threshold climbs, precision rises and recall falls. Which point you pick is an application judgment call, not something cross- validation chooses — a cheap, safe treatment for a dangerous disease argues for high recall (low threshold); a costly, invasive one argues for high precision. precision_recall_curve gives you every point on that trade-off at once, and classification_report prints the whole per-class table:

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, classification_report

precisions, recalls, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(yte, proba)
# plot precisions vs recalls to see the full trade-off frontier

print(classification_report(yte, yhat, digits=3))

The report's row for class 1 restates our by-hand precision 0.939 / recall 0.568 / F1 0.708 — now you know exactly where each number came from.

docs.title: 9. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code above, to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away. Do at least the first two.

1. Change the split ratios. Re-run Section 1 with a 70/15/15 split. Does the chosen degree from Section 3 change? (Smaller CV sets give noisier J_cv.)

Solution 
n_train, n_cv = int(0.7 * m), int(0.15 * m)
tr, cv, te = idx[:n_train], idx[n_train:n_train + n_cv], idx[n_train + n_cv:]
X_train, y_train = X[tr], y[tr]
X_cv, y_cv, X_test, y_test = X[cv], y[cv], X[te], y[te]
best_d = min(range(1, 11), key=lambda d: J(PolyReg(d).fit(X_train, y_train), X_cv, y_cv))
print("chosen degree:", best_d)   # still a low degree — the U bottoms out near the true 2

2. Extend the high-variance learning curve. In Section 5, add n = 100 and confirm the train–CV gap keeps closing — proof that more data is still paying off.

Solution 
for n in (15, 30, 60, 100, 120):
    model = PolyReg(12).fit(X_train[:n], y_train[:n])
    gap = J(model, X_cv, y_cv) - J(model, X_train[:n], y_train[:n])
    print(f"n={n:3d}   gap(J_cv − J_train) = {gap:.3f}")   # gap shrinks as n rises

3. Turn the bias/variance dial with regularization. Ridge adds an L2 penalty — more penalty = simpler model = more bias, less variance. Swap poly_model for a high-degree Ridge and watch a big alpha tame the overfit.

Solution 
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
for alpha in (0.0001, 1.0, 100.0):
    model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                          PolynomialFeatures(12, include_bias=False),
                          Ridge(alpha=alpha)).fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"alpha={alpha:8}: J_train={J(model, X_train, y_train):.3f}  J_cv={J(model, X_cv, y_cv):.3f}")
# tiny alpha → overfits (J_cv ≫ J_train); huge alpha → underfits (both high)

4. Read a stricter threshold. In Section 8, add t = 0.9 and read off precision and recall. How far does recall fall when you only act on near-certainties?

Solution 
pred = (proba >= 0.9).astype(int)
print("precision:", round(precision_score(yte, pred, zero_division=0), 3),
      " recall:", round(recall_score(yte, pred), 3))   # precision high, recall drops further

5. Widen the accuracy trap. In Section 7, regenerate the data with weights=[0.99, 0.01] (1% positives) and re-fit. Watch recall collapse while accuracy stays flatteringly high.

Solution 
Xc, yc = make_classification(n_samples=5000, n_features=10, n_informative=6,
                             n_redundant=0, weights=[0.99, 0.01],
                             class_sep=1.0, random_state=1)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.3, stratify=yc, random_state=1)
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(Xtr, ytr)
yhat = clf.predict(Xte)
print("accuracy:", round((yhat == yte).mean(), 4),
      " recall:", round(recall_score(yte, yhat), 3))   # high accuracy, dismal recall

docs.title: C2 · W4 — Decision Trees, Random Forests & Boosting, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 2 · Week 4 lessons that the code builds on — what a tree is, how it measures purity, how it picks a split, and the two ensembles that make trees win competitions:

  • Decision Tree Model
  • Measuring Purity → Choosing a Split: Information Gain
  • Random Forest Algorithm → XGBoost

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

A decision tree is just a game of 20 questions: keep asking the single most informative yes/no question until you're confident of the answer. The whole trick is defining "most informative" as a number the computer can optimize. Let's build it from the inside out:

  1. From scratch — write the impurity and information-gain formulas from the lessons as a few lines of NumPy, then use them to find the best question to ask (a one-node tree).
  2. The library way — DecisionTreeClassifier, which does exactly that recursively.
  3. The ensembles — see one tree overfit, then fix it two ways: random forests (many trees vote) and boosting / XGBoost (each tree fixes the last one's mistakes). Both are what you'd actually reach for on the job.

The from-scratch part uses the cat dataset from the lessons so the numbers match what you saw on the slides. The library part switches to a 2-D dataset so you can watch trees overfit.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
First, the cat dataset from the lesson — 10 animals, three binary features (ear shape pointy=1/floppy=0, face shape round=1/not=0, whiskers present=1/absent=0), and the label y = "is it a cat?". Five cats, five dogs:

import numpy as np

#            ear face whisk
X = np.array([[1,  1,  1],    # cat
              [0,  0,  1],    # cat
              [0,  1,  0],    # dog
              [1,  0,  1],    # dog
              [1,  1,  1],    # cat
              [1,  1,  0],    # cat
              [0,  0,  0],    # dog
              [1,  1,  0],    # cat
              [0,  1,  0],    # dog
              [0,  1,  0]])   # dog
y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0])
feature_names = ["ear shape", "face shape", "whiskers"]

The root has 5 cats out of 10, so p₁ = 0.5 — a perfect 50/50 mix, the most impure a set can be. Our job is to ask questions that carve out purer subsets.

docs.title: 1. Measuring purity from scratch
docs.text:
To choose splits by purity you need to quantify it. The lesson's tool is entropy: a number that's 0 when a set is all one class (pure) and peaks at 1 for a 50/50 mix. With p₁ the fraction of cats and p₀ = 1 − p₁, the formula from the slide is

\[H(p_1) = -p_1\log_2 p_1 - (1-p_1)\log_2(1-p_1),\]

which is a direct transcription into NumPy:

def entropy(y):
    if len(y) == 0:
        return 0.0
    p1 = y.mean()                       # fraction of class 1 (cats)
    if p1 == 0 or p1 == 1:
        return 0.0                      # pure set: convention 0·log0 = 0
    return -p1 * np.log2(p1) - (1 - p1) * np.log2(1 - p1)

print(entropy(y))                       # → 1.0, the 50/50 root is maximally impure
print(entropy(np.array([1, 1, 1])))     # → 0.0, all cats: perfectly pure
print(round(entropy(np.array([1,1,1,1,1,0])), 3))   # 5 cats/1 dog → ~0.65

Those middle numbers match the slide exactly. Real libraries usually default to a close cousin, Gini impurity — the chance you'd mislabel a random example if you guessed by the set's class proportions:

\[G = 1 - p_1^2 - p_0^2.\] 
def gini(y):
    if len(y) == 0:
        return 0.0
    p1 = y.mean()
    return 1 - p1**2 - (1 - p1)**2

print(gini(y))                          # → 0.5, its own peak for a 50/50 mix

Entropy and Gini have nearly the same shape (both zero when pure, both maximal at 50/50), so they almost always grow the same tree. Gini is a hair cheaper to compute, which is why scikit-learn uses it by default; entropy is one keyword away. Use entropy below so the numbers line up with the lessons.

docs.title: 2. Scoring a split: information gain
docs.text:
A split sends some examples left and some right, each branch with its own entropy. You don't just average the two — you take a weighted average, weighting each branch by the fraction of examples that land in it (a branch holding more animals matters more). The value of the split is how much that weighted entropy drops below the parent's — the information gain:

\[\text{gain} = H(\text{parent}) - \Big(w_{\text{left}}H(\text{left}) + w_{\text{right}}H(\text{right})\Big).\]

For a binary feature, "left" is the rows where the feature is 0 and "right" where it's 1:

def information_gain(X, y, feature):
    col = X[:, feature]
    left, right = y[col == 0], y[col == 1]
    n = len(y)
    weighted = (len(left) / n) * entropy(left) + (len(right) / n) * entropy(right)
    return entropy(y) - weighted            # drop in impurity

Now score every feature and see which question is most informative:

for f, name in enumerate(feature_names):
    print(f"{name:12s} gain = {information_gain(X, y, f):.3f}")
# ear shape    gain = 0.278   ← the winner
# face shape   gain = 0.035
# whiskers     gain = 0.125

Ear shape wins with gain ≈ 0.28 — exactly the slide's number. Splitting on it gives a left branch (floppy) that's mostly dogs and a right branch (pointy) that's mostly cats: p₁ = 1/5 and 4/5, each weighted 5/10. That's the whole engine.

Measuring the drop rather than the raw branch entropy also gives you a free stopping rule: if the best available split barely lowers entropy, don't bother — leaving the node as a leaf keeps the tree small and fights overfitting.

docs.title: 3. From gain to a tree: one greedy split
docs.text:
The full algorithm (scikit-learn calls it CART) is just this: pick the split with the highest gain, then recurse on each branch, stopping when a branch is pure or you hit a depth limit. It's greedy — it grabs the best split now without checking whether a different early split would pay off deeper down — which is fast and usually good enough. Here we do the first split, the one that becomes the root:

best = max(range(X.shape[1]), key=lambda f: information_gain(X, y, f))
print(f"root question: split on '{feature_names[best]}'")

col = X[:, best]
print("  left  (floppy):", y[col == 0], "→ predict", round(y[col == 0].mean()))
print("  right (pointy):", y[col == 1], "→ predict", round(y[col == 1].mean()))

Each leaf predicts its majority class (round(mean) of a 0/1 array). Recurse the same information_gain search on the two branches and you've hand-built a decision tree — but you'd never do that in practice, because the library does it faster and prunes for you.

docs.title: 4. The library way — DecisionTreeClassifier
docs.text:
To watch a tree actually overfit, switch to a 2-D dataset with curved structure and some noise, split into train/test:

from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

Xm, ym = make_moons(n_samples=500, noise=0.30, random_state=42)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(Xm, ym, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

Grow a tree with no depth limit and it will keep splitting until every training leaf is pure:

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42)      # no max_depth → grows all the way
tree.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"train {tree.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f}   test {tree.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# train 1.000   test 0.856  ← memorized the training set, gap = overfitting

Perfect on training, worse on test: the classic overfitting signature. An unconstrained tree carves the plane into tiny boxes around individual noisy points. The cure is pruning — cap the depth so it can't:

pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
pruned.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"train {pruned.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f}   test {pruned.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# train 0.899   test 0.896  ← lower training score, but the gap closed

You can read exactly what it learned — tree.feature_importances_, or sklearn.tree.plot_tree(pruned) to draw the boxes. That readability is why trees are called "white-box" models. But one tree is twitchy: change a few training points and the whole structure can flip. The fix is to stop relying on a single tree.

docs.title: 5. Ensemble #1 — Random Forests (bagging + random features)
docs.text:
The wisdom of the crowd: ask one expert and you get one opinion; ask a thousand so-so predictors and average them, and the errors cancel out. For trees this is a random forest. Two ingredients from the lesson, both easy to write:

  1. Bagging — for each tree, draw a bootstrap sample (sample the training rows with replacement, same size m), so every tree sees a slightly different dataset.
  2. Random features — at each split, consider only a random subset of k ≈ √n features, so the trees don't all latch onto the same dominant split and end up clones.

Here's the whole algorithm by hand — a loop of shallow-ish trees, then a majority vote:

from scipy.stats import mode

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
m = len(X_tr)
trees = []
for b in range(100):                                  # B = 100 trees
    idx = rng.integers(0, m, m)                       # bootstrap: sample rows WITH replacement
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_features="sqrt", random_state=b)   # random √n features/split
    t.fit(X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx])
    trees.append(t)

votes = np.array([t.predict(X_te) for t in trees])    # (100 trees, n_test)
y_pred = mode(votes, axis=0, keepdims=False).mode      # majority vote per example
print(f"hand-rolled forest test {(y_pred == y_te).mean():.3f}")
# hand-rolled forest test 0.904  ← beats the single tree's 0.856

That's genuinely all a random forest is. scikit-learn wraps it in one estimator (and does the same thing, faster and in parallel):

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, max_features="sqrt", random_state=42)
forest.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"forest test {forest.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")   # ~0.90, and far more stable than one tree

More trees never hurt accuracy, but you hit diminishing returns fast — 100–128 is the sweet spot; 1,000 just burns compute for a rounding error. Because bagging already averages over many small perturbations of the data, the forest barely moves when you nudge the training set — that robustness is the payoff.

docs.title: 6. Ensemble #2 — Boosting / XGBoost
docs.text:
A forest builds its trees independently and averages them. Boosting builds them in sequence, each new tree focusing on the examples the ensemble still gets wrong — like practicing piano by drilling only the bars you keep fumbling, instead of replaying the whole piece. Trees are added one at a time, each correcting its predecessors' residual mistakes. scikit-learn ships this as GradientBoostingClassifier:

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1,
                                max_depth=2, random_state=42)   # small trees, added in sequence
gb.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"gradient boosting test {gb.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")     # ~0.90

Note the trees are shallow (max_depth=2) — boosting wants many weak learners, not a few strong ones, and learning_rate shrinks each tree's contribution so the ensemble improves in small, safe steps.

XGBoost ("Extreme Gradient Boosting") is the industrial version of this idea and the most common tree implementation in production and on Kaggle: fast, sensible defaults, and built-in regularization to keep it from overfitting. Same three-line API (pip install xgboost first):

from xgboost import XGBClassifier                   # XGBRegressor for regression targets

xgb = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=2)
xgb.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"xgboost test {xgb.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")  # competitive with / beats the others

Under the hood XGBoost weights the misclassified examples rather than literally resampling them, but the "focus on the mistakes" intuition is exactly right. For everyday tabular data, a random forest or XGBoost is very often the strongest thing you can reach for — no feature scaling, handles mixed feature types, and hard to beat.

docs.title: 7. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code you already ran above, meant to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away if you get stuck. Do at least the first two.

1. Swap entropy for Gini. Re-rank the three cat features using gini instead of entropy in information_gain. Does ear shape still win? (It should — the two criteria almost always agree.)

Solution 
def gain_gini(X, y, feature):
    col = X[:, feature]
    left, right = y[col == 0], y[col == 1]
    n = len(y)
    weighted = (len(left)/n)*gini(left) + (len(right)/n)*gini(right)
    return gini(y) - weighted

for f, name in enumerate(feature_names):
    print(f"{name:12s} {gain_gini(X, y, f):.3f}")
# ear shape still has the largest drop — same winner as entropy

2. Sweep the tree depth. Loop max_depth from 1 to 10, printing train and test accuracy for each. Watch the train score march to 1.0 while test peaks and then sags — that's the overfitting curve in one table.

Solution 
for d in range(1, 11):
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=d, random_state=42).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"depth {d:2d}: train {t.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f}  test {t.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# train keeps rising; test tops out around depth 3-5 then drifts down

3. One tree vs. a hundred. Set n_estimators=1 in RandomForestClassifier, fit, and compare its test score to the 100-tree forest. Then feel the stability: refit each a few times with different random_states and watch how much more the single tree's score jumps around.

Solution 
for n in (1, 5, 100):
    f = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n, random_state=42).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"{n:3d} trees: test {f.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# accuracy climbs and then plateaus; the 1-tree score is also far twitchier run to run

4. Kill the random-feature trick. Set max_features=None in your hand-rolled forest (so every tree considers all features at each split — pure bagging). Compare the vote accuracy. Removing the feature randomness makes the trees more alike, so averaging helps a little less.

Solution 
trees = []
for b in range(100):
    idx = rng.integers(0, m, m)
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_features=None, random_state=b).fit(X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx])
    trees.append(t)
votes = np.array([t.predict(X_te) for t in trees])
y_pred = mode(votes, axis=0, keepdims=False).mode
print(f"bagging-only test {(y_pred == y_te).mean():.3f}")   # usually a touch below the √n forest

5. Turn the boosting knobs. Try learning_rate in (0.01, 0.1, 1.0) on GradientBoostingClassifier. A tiny rate under-fits in 100 trees; a large one overshoots. This is the same learning-rate trade-off you met in gradient descent.

Solution 
for lr in (0.01, 0.1, 1.0):
    g = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=lr,
                                   max_depth=2, random_state=42).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    print(f"lr={lr}: train {g.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f}  test {g.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}")
# 0.01 underfits (both low); 0.1 is the sweet spot; 1.0 overfits (train↑, test↓)

docs.title: C3 · W1 — K-Means Clustering & Anomaly Detection, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

You'll get the most out of this once you've watched the Course 3 · Week 1 lessons it builds on — the two clustering steps, the cost they minimize, and the Gaussian model behind anomaly detection:

  • K-means Intuition → The K-means Algorithm
  • Optimization Objective (the distortion cost)
  • Gaussian (Normal) Distribution
  • Anomaly Detection Algorithm

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in whatever order you like — but this is the theory it turns into code.

This week has two unsupervised algorithms, and they rhyme: both look at unlabeled data and ask "what does normal look like here?" We'll build both from scratch in NumPy, watch the math from the lessons turn into a few lines of code, and then swap in the library version you'd actually reach for on the job.

  1. K-means — the "assign, then move" loop, hand-rolled, then scikit-learn's KMeans.
  2. Anomaly detection — fit a Gaussian to each feature, multiply the densities, flag the points that land in the tails.

No labels anywhere. That's the whole point of unsupervised learning.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
For clustering we'll make three loose blobs of points. Because we placed the centers, we can check whether K-means rediscovers them.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)          # fixed seed → reproducible "random" data

centers = np.array([[0.0, 0.0], [5.0, 5.0], [0.0, 6.0]])
X = np.vstack([c + rng.standard_normal((60, 2)) for c in centers])   # 180 points, 2 features
print(X.shape)                           # (180, 2)

X has m = 180 rows (examples) and n = 2 columns (features) — exactly the x⁽ⁱ⁾ ∈ ℝⁿ setup from the lesson. K-means never sees centers; it only sees X.

docs.title: 1. K-means from scratch — the two steps
docs.text:
The algorithm is just two operations repeated until nothing changes:

  • Step 1 — assign. Give each point the label of its nearest centroid (c⁽ⁱ⁾ = argmin_k ‖x⁽ⁱ⁾ − μ_k‖²).
  • Step 2 — move. Slide each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it.

docs.title: Step 1 as code
docs.text:
We need, for every point, the distance to every centroid — then pick the smallest. NumPy broadcasting does all m × K distances at once:

def assign(X, centroids):
    # X[:, None, :] is (m, 1, n); centroids[None, :, :] is (1, K, n) → broadcast to (m, K, n)
    dists = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :], axis=2)   # (m, K) distances
    return dists.argmin(axis=1)          # index of the closest centroid for each point

The squared norm and the plain norm pick the same nearest centroid, so we can use either; np.linalg.norm is the readable choice here.

docs.title: Step 2 as code
docs.text:
Each new centroid is the column-wise average of its members:

def move(X, labels, K):
    return np.array([X[labels == k].mean(axis=0) for k in range(K)])   # (K, n) new centroids

If cluster 1 owns examples 1, 5, 6, 10, this returns their mean — literally μ₁ = ¼(x⁽¹⁾ + x⁽⁵⁾ + x⁽⁶⁾ + x⁽¹⁰⁾) from the lesson.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
Initialize by picking K actual data points as the starting centroids (Ng's random init), then alternate the two steps:

K = 3
centroids = X[rng.choice(len(X), K, replace=False)].copy()   # K random points as init

for _ in range(10):
    labels = assign(X, centroids)        # Step 1
    centroids = move(X, labels, K)       # Step 2

print(np.round(centroids, 1))            # ≈ the [0,0], [5,5], [0,6] we started from

Ten passes is plenty here — K-means usually converges in a handful of iterations, when no point changes label and the centroids stop moving.

docs.title: 2. The distortion cost — and watching it fall
docs.text:
K-means isn't wandering randomly; it's minimizing the distortion from the optimization lesson — the average squared distance from each point to its centroid:

\[J = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\big\|x^{(i)} - \mu_{c^{(i)}}\big\|^2.\] 
def distortion(X, labels, centroids):
    return np.mean(np.sum((X - centroids[labels])**2, axis=1))   # mean squared dist to own centroid

centroids[labels] is a slick move: it builds an (m, n) array where row i is the centroid assigned to point i. Now re-run the loop and print J each iteration:

centroids = X[rng.choice(len(X), K, replace=False)].copy()
for step in range(10):
    labels = assign(X, centroids)
    centroids = move(X, labels, K)
    print(step, round(distortion(X, labels, centroids), 3))   # monotonically DOWN

The number goes down every step and then flattens. That's the guarantee from the lesson: each step provably reduces (never increases) J — Step 1 can only lower it by moving points to closer centroids, Step 2 can only lower it by re-centering. If you ever see J rise, you have a bug.

Why this matters later: this is the same "define a cost, then relentlessly drive it down" pattern as supervised learning — K-means just uses its two-step update instead of gradient descent. Same skeleton, different engine.

docs.title: 3. How many clusters? The elbow method
docs.text:
K-means needs K up front, and often there's no single right answer. One diagnostic (Géron's elbow, which Ng mentions but rarely relies on): run K-means for a range of K, plot the distortion, and look for the bend where extra clusters stop buying you much.

def kmeans_distortion(X, K, iters=10):
    centroids = X[rng.choice(len(X), K, replace=False)].copy()
    for _ in range(iters):
        labels = assign(X, centroids)
        centroids = move(X, labels, K)
    return distortion(X, labels, centroids)

for K in range(1, 8):
    print(K, round(kmeans_distortion(X, K), 2))   # drops fast to K=3, then only slowly

The distortion falls steeply up to K = 3 (our true number of blobs) and then only crawls lower — that flattening is the "elbow." Note what does not work: picking K to minimize distortion just keeps climbing to the largest K, since more centroids always fit tighter.

docs.title: 4. The library way — scikit-learn
docs.text:
In practice you don't hand-roll any of this. scikit-learn's KMeans does the loop for you, runs it several times from different starts, and keeps the best:

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=42)
labels = km.fit_predict(X)
print(km.cluster_centers_.round(1))      # same three centers you found by hand
print(km.inertia_)                       # the cost — see the note below

Two details worth knowing:

  • inertia_ is the distortion — but summed, not averaged. scikit-learn reports Σ‖x⁽ⁱ⁾ − μ_c⁽ⁱ⁾‖² (Géron's "inertia"), i.e. our distortion(...) × m. Same quantity, no 1/m. Multiply our value by len(X) and they match.
  • n_init=10 fixes the biggest weakness of the from-scratch version. A single unlucky random init can settle into a bad local optimum. Running 10 inits and keeping the lowest-inertia result (the default uses the smarter k-means++ seeding, which spreads the initial centroids apart) makes that failure rare.

Predict the cluster for new points with km.predict([[5, 5]]), and read the final centroids off km.cluster_centers_.

docs.title: 5. Anomaly detection from scratch — a Gaussian per feature
docs.text:
Second algorithm, same unsupervised spirit. We model what normal looks like with a Gaussian on each feature, multiply the per-feature densities into one probability p(x), and flag anything whose p(x) is tiny.

Fresh dataset: think server-monitoring, two features (say throughput and latency), mostly normal with a few genuine outliers bolted on.

X_normal = rng.standard_normal((300, 2)) * [2.0, 1.0] + [10.0, 5.0]   # the "healthy" cloud
X_anom   = np.array([[20.0, 12.0], [0.0, 12.0], [18.0, -1.0]])        # 3 planted anomalies
Xa = np.vstack([X_normal, X_anom])

docs.title: Fit μ and σ² per feature
docs.text:
Straight from the Gaussian lesson: μⱼ is the average of feature j, σ²ⱼ its average squared deviation. In NumPy that's one call each — and np.var divides by m by default, which is exactly Ng's maximum-likelihood estimate (not the m − 1 version):

mu  = X_normal.mean(axis=0)              # per-feature mean  μ_j   → shape (n,)
var = X_normal.var(axis=0)               # per-feature var   σ²_j  (ddof=0 → divides by m)
print(mu.round(2), var.round(2))         # ≈ [10, 5] and ≈ [4, 1]

We fit on X_normal only — the model's job is to learn "normal," so we don't let the anomalies pollute the parameters.

docs.title: The density product p(x)
docs.text:
The Gaussian formula and the product-over-features from the lesson, verbatim in code:

\[p(\vec{x}) = \prod_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_j}\, e^{-\frac{(x_j-\mu_j)^2}{2\sigma_j^2}}.\] 
def gaussian_p(X, mu, var):
    coef = 1.0 / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi * var)          # the 1/(√(2π)σ) factor, per feature
    exponent = np.exp(-(X - mu)**2 / (2 * var))     # the bell-curve drop-off, per feature
    return np.prod(coef * exponent, axis=1)         # multiply features → one p(x) per row

Multiplying is what makes a point anomalous if it's unusual on any feature — an extreme value in even one column tanks the whole product.

docs.title: Threshold with ε
docs.text:
Flag a point as an anomaly when p(x) < ε. Pick ε just below the least-likely normal point so the healthy cloud stays in but the outliers fall out:

p = gaussian_p(Xa, mu, var)
epsilon = p[:300].min() * 0.5            # a hair under the most borderline normal point
flagged = p < epsilon

print("anomalies found at rows:", np.where(flagged)[0])   # → 300, 301, 302: the planted ones
print("false alarms in normal set:", flagged[:300].sum()) # → 0

The three flagged rows are exactly the ones we planted, with no false alarms in the healthy cloud. In a real system you'd tune ε on a small labeled validation set (that's the developing and evaluating lesson) rather than eyeballing it.

docs.title: 6. The library way — reuse SciPy's Gaussian
docs.text:
You don't need a library to run this — the from-scratch version is already three lines — but you also shouldn't re-type the bell-curve formula every time. SciPy's norm.pdf is the same p(xⱼ; μⱼ, σ²ⱼ), so the whole density is one .prod:

from scipy.stats import norm

p_scipy = norm.pdf(Xa, loc=mu, scale=np.sqrt(var)).prod(axis=1)   # note: scale is σ, not σ²
print(np.allclose(p_scipy, gaussian_p(Xa, mu, var)))              # True — identical numbers

Watch the one gotcha: norm.pdf wants the standard deviation σ (scale=np.sqrt(var)), not the variance. Beyond this per-feature model, scikit-learn ships heavier anomaly detectors (IsolationForest, EllipticEnvelope) for when features interact — but the independent- Gaussian model here is the one Ng teaches, and it's a genuinely strong baseline.

docs.title: 7. Your turn
docs.text:
These aren't new exercises — each is a small tweak to the code you already ran above, meant to build intuition by poking at it. Try each yourself first; the solution is one click away if you get stuck. Do at least the first two.

1. Confirm scratch and scikit-learn agree on the cost. km.inertia_ is the summed distortion; your distortion(...) is the mean. Multiply yours by len(X) and compare.

Solution 
my_labels = assign(X, km.cluster_centers_)
my_sum = distortion(X, my_labels, km.cluster_centers_) * len(X)
print("scratch (summed):", round(my_sum, 2))
print("sklearn inertia_:", round(km.inertia_, 2))   # essentially equal

2. Feel a bad random init. Force a single, unlucky start (n_init=1) with a couple of different seeds and print inertia_ — some seeds land in a worse local optimum than others.

Solution 
for seed in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    km_bad = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init="random", n_init=1, random_state=seed).fit(X)
    print(seed, round(km_bad.inertia_, 1))   # values vary — that's why n_init > 1 matters

3. Tighten and loosen ε. Halve epsilon, then double it, and count how many points get flagged each time — the classic precision/recall knob of anomaly detection.

Solution 
for factor in (0.25, 0.5, 2.0, 5.0):
    eps = p[:300].min() * factor
    print(f"factor {factor}: {(p < eps).sum()} flagged")   # bigger ε → more (incl. false) alarms

4. Break the independence assumption. Add a third feature that's just feature0 + feature1 (perfectly correlated) and re-fit — the per-feature model still runs, it just can't "see" the correlation. Confirm the planted anomalies are still caught.

Solution 
Xa3 = np.c_[Xa, Xa[:, 0] + Xa[:, 1]]        # add a redundant, correlated 3rd feature
mu3, var3 = X_normal.mean(0), X_normal.var(0)
mu3 = np.r_[mu3, (X_normal[:,0]+X_normal[:,1]).mean()]
var3 = np.r_[var3, (X_normal[:,0]+X_normal[:,1]).var()]
p3 = gaussian_p(Xa3, mu3, var3)
print(np.where(p3 < p3[:300].min() * 0.5)[0])   # 300,301,302 still flagged

docs.title: C3 · W2 — PCA & Collaborative-Filtering Recommenders, in Code
docs.text:
Recommended before this lab

This week bundles two unsupervised ideas — PCA (squash many features into 2–3) and collaborative filtering (learn recommendations from a table full of holes). Watch these first and the code below is just the math written out:

  • Reducing the Number of Features → PCA Algorithm → PCA in Code
  • Collaborative Filtering Algorithm

Not strict prerequisites — do the lab in any order — but this is the theory it turns into code.

This lab has two independent halves, matching the two topics of the week:

  • Part I — PCA. Find the axis your data actually varies along, then throw the rest away. We build it two ways from scratch (covariance + eigenvectors, and the SVD) so you see they land on the same axes, then do it in one line with scikit-learn.
  • Part II — Collaborative filtering. Given a ratings table where most cells are blank, learn a latent-factor vector for every user and every item at once, purely by gradient descent — then read off predictions for the blanks.

A note on the recommender. PCA is textbook material (Géron Ch. 8, Raschka Ch. 5). Matrix-factorization recommenders are not — neither book covers them. So Part II is built from first principles straight out of Ng's lecture: define the cost, take its gradient, roll downhill. It's the same "measure a cost, follow the slope" engine from the very first lab.

docs.title: 0. Setup and some data
docs.text:
We'll make a 2-D cloud that's really 1-D in disguise: both features track one hidden "size" variable, plus a little noise. PCA should discover that hidden axis.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
m = 200
t = rng.standard_normal(m)                    # the hidden 1-D signal
X = np.c_[3 * t + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(m),   # feature 1 tracks t strongly
          2 * t + 0.5 * rng.standard_normal(m)]   # feature 2 tracks t too

X is (200, 2). Plot it and you'd see a fat diagonal streak — the two features are correlated, so almost all the spread lies along one diagonal direction. PCA's whole job is to find that direction.

docs.title: 1. Step zero: center the data
docs.text:
PCA is about variance (spread), and variance is measured around the mean. So every route starts by subtracting each feature's mean — exactly the "normalize features to zero mean" preprocessing step from the lecture. (If your features were on wildly different scales — GDP in trillions vs. a count under 100 — you'd also divide by the standard deviation first. Ours are comparable, so centering is enough.)

X_c = X - X.mean(axis=0)                       # zero-centered; PCA assumes this

docs.title: 2. Route A — covariance matrix + eigenvectors (Raschka's from-scratch recipe)
docs.text:
Here's the classic derivation. "Which direction has the most spread?" is answered by the covariance matrix — a small n×n table (here 2×2) whose entries measure how each pair of features varies together. Its eigenvectors are the principal-component axes, and each eigenvector's eigenvalue is the variance along that axis. Bigger eigenvalue → more important axis.

cov = np.cov(X_c.T)                            # 2×2 covariance matrix
eig_vals, eig_vecs = np.linalg.eigh(cov)       # eigh: for symmetric matrices, real answers

# eigh returns them smallest-first — flip to biggest-first so PC1 comes first
order = np.argsort(eig_vals)[::-1]
eig_vals, eig_vecs = eig_vals[order], eig_vecs[:, order]

print("variance per axis:", eig_vals)          # first number >> second
print("PC1 direction:", eig_vecs[:, 0])        # the unit vector u from the lecture

Use np.linalg.eigh (not eig): a covariance matrix is symmetric, and eigh is the numerically stable version that always returns real eigenvalues. The columns of eig_vecs are the unit-length axes — the same u = [0.71, 0.71]-style vector the lesson projected onto.

The principal component is eig_vecs[:, 0]: the axis with the largest eigenvalue, i.e. the direction the data is most spread out along. The second column is automatically at 90° to it — eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix are orthogonal, which is why PCA's axes always come out perpendicular.

docs.title: 3. Route B — the SVD (Géron's route, and what scikit-learn actually does)
docs.text:
Building the covariance matrix and eigen-decomposing it is one valid recipe, but it's not how production code does it. There's a single matrix factorization — the singular value decomposition — that hands you the principal components directly from the centered data, skipping the covariance matrix entirely and with better numerical behavior:

\[X_c = U\,\Sigma\,V^\top\]

The rows of Vᵀ are the principal components, already sorted best-first.

U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_c, full_matrices=False)

print("PC1 direction:", Vt[0])                 # same axis Route A found (maybe sign-flipped)

Both routes describe the same line. The only thing that can differ is a sign flip — the axis [0.83, 0.55] and [-0.83, -0.55] are the same line pointing opposite ways, and which one you get depends on the library version. That's expected and harmless (just retrain any downstream model whenever you refit PCA).

The singular values s even carry the variances: s**2 is proportional to the eigenvalues from Route A.

docs.title: 4. Projecting down (and reconstructing back)
docs.text:
To actually reduce 2-D → 1-D, project every centered point onto the top axis — which, from the lesson, is just a dot product with the unit vector. Stack the top k axes into a matrix W and it's one matrix multiply for the whole dataset:

\[Z = X_c\,W\] 
W = Vt[:1].T                                   # keep the top 1 component → shape (2, 1)
Z = X_c @ W                                     # every point becomes ONE number
print(Z[:3].ravel())                            # e.g. [-1.31, 2.99, -3.09]

Each 2-number example is now a single number — its position along the principal axis. To go the other way (reconstruction), multiply back and add the mean you subtracted:

X_recon = Z @ W.T + X.mean(axis=0)             # approximate the original 2-D points
print("reconstruction MSE:", np.mean((X - X_recon) ** 2))   # tiny — we lost almost nothing

You can't recover the originals exactly (the second dimension was thrown away), but because that dimension held almost no variance, the reconstruction is nearly perfect — which is the whole promise of PCA.

docs.title: 5. How much did we keep? Explained variance ratio
docs.text:
The honest question after any dimensionality cut is "what fraction of the information survived?" That's the explained variance ratio: each axis's variance divided by the total. From the SVD's singular values:

ratio = s**2 / (s**2).sum()
print(ratio)                                    # ≈ [0.976, 0.024]

The first axis alone explains ~98% of the spread — so collapsing this data to one number loses ~2%. On real data you'd take the cumulative sum and keep enough axes to reach, say, 95%: d = np.argmax(np.cumsum(ratio) >= 0.95) + 1.

docs.title: 6. The library way — scikit-learn
docs.text:
Nobody hand-rolls the above at work. scikit-learn does all of Parts 1–5 — centering, SVD, projection, variance accounting — behind three lines:

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=1)
Z_sk = pca.fit_transform(X)                     # note: pass the RAW X — fit centers it for you
print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)            # ≈ [0.976]
print(Z_sk[:3].ravel())                         # same numbers as our Z (up to a sign flip)

Two conveniences to notice: fit_transform centers the data for you (so you feed raw X, not X_c), and pca.components_ holds Wᵀ — one row per principal component. You can also pass a float, PCA(n_components=0.95), to say "keep however many axes I need for 95% of the variance" and let it pick the number.

What is PCA good for today? Ng's honest take: mainly visualization — squash 50 features to 2–3 and scatter-plot them to eyeball structure. The old uses (compressing data, speeding up training) matter far less now that storage is cheap and deep nets happily eat high-dimensional input directly.

docs.title: 7. The setup: a ratings table full of holes
docs.text:
A recommender's raw material is a big ratings matrix Y: rows are movies, columns are users, and cell Y[i, j] is how many stars user j gave movie i. The catch — most cells are empty, because no one has seen most movies. We track which cells are filled with a mask R (R[i, j] = 1 if rated). The goal: predict the blanks.

Instead of a real dataset, we'll fabricate a low-rank one so we can check our answers. We invent secret feature vectors for every movie and every user, multiply them to get the "true" complete table, then hide 60% of the cells and see if the algorithm can rediscover them.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_movies, n_users, k_true = 20, 15, 3
true_X = rng.standard_normal((n_movies, k_true))   # secret movie features
true_W = rng.standard_normal((n_users,  k_true))   # secret user tastes
true_b = rng.standard_normal(n_users)              # secret per-user bias

full = true_X @ true_W.T + true_b                  # the complete "true" ratings
R = (rng.random((n_movies, n_users)) < 0.4).astype(float)   # observe only ~40%
Y = full * R                                       # the table we're actually handed
print("observed", int(R.sum()), "of", R.size, "cells")   # ~120 of 300

(Real ratings are integers 1–5; ours are continuous for simplicity — the algorithm is identical.)

docs.title: 8. The model and the cost, from scratch
docs.text:
From Using Per-Item Features, the predicted rating of movie i by user j is a dot product of a movie-feature vector x⁽ⁱ⁾ and a user-parameter vector w⁽ʲ⁾, plus a per-user bias:

\[\hat{y}(i,j) = \vec{w}^{(j)}\cdot\vec{x}^{(i)} + b^{(j)}\]

The twist of collaborative filtering: we know neither the x's nor the w's. We learn both at the same time. As one matrix multiply, all predictions at once are X @ W.T + b:

def predict(X, W, b):
    return X @ W.T + b            # (n_movies, k) @ (k, n_users) → (n_movies, n_users)

The cost is the squared error over the observed cells only — the mask R zeros out the blanks so they never contribute — plus L2 regularization on both factor tables:

def cost(X, W, b, Y, R, lam):
    err = (predict(X, W, b) - Y) * R           # error, but ONLY where we have a rating
    reg = 0.5 * lam * ((X**2).sum() + (W**2).sum())
    return 0.5 * (err**2).sum() + reg

That * R is the entire trick for handling missing data: an unrated cell contributes exactly zero to the loss, so gradient descent simply ignores it.

docs.title: 9. Gradient descent, from scratch
docs.text:
Same engine as every other lab: take the slope of the cost with respect to every parameter table, and step downhill. Differentiating the masked squared error gives clean matrix gradients (with E = (predict − Y) · R the masked error):

  • dX = E @ W + λX
  • dW = Eᵀ @ X + λW
  • db = E.sum(axis=0) (no regularization on the bias)
n = 3                                           # how many latent features to learn
X = rng.standard_normal((n_movies, n)) * 0.1    # start small & random
W = rng.standard_normal((n_users,  n)) * 0.1
b = np.zeros(n_users)
eta, lam = 0.01, 0.1

for epoch in range(3000):
    E  = (predict(X, W, b) - Y) * R             # masked error, shared by all gradients
    dX = E @ W       + lam * X
    dW = E.T @ X     + lam * W
    db = E.sum(axis=0)
    X -= eta * dX                               # simultaneous update of all three
    W -= eta * dW
    b -= eta * db
    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print(epoch, "cost", round(cost(X, W, b, Y, R, lam), 3))

All three tables update together from the same error E — the "collaborative" part: every user's ratings help pin down each movie's features, which in turn sharpen every user's predictions.

Now the payoff — check it against the cells we hid:

P = predict(X, W, b)
train_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((P - full)[R == 1] ** 2))   # cells it trained on
held_rmse  = np.sqrt(np.mean((P - full)[R == 0] ** 2))   # cells it NEVER saw
print("train RMSE", round(train_rmse, 3), " held-out RMSE", round(held_rmse, 3))

You'll see something like train RMSE 0.08 held-out RMSE 1.22. The held-out error is higher (it's genuinely predicting unseen ratings) but it crushes the naive baseline of "guess each movie's average" (~1.90) — from ~120 known cells it reconstructed the 180 unknown ones. That is a recommender. To recommend for user j, sort column P[:, j] and take the movies they haven't seen with the highest predicted rating.

New users get sensible defaults for free-ish. The lecture's mean-normalization trick — subtract each movie's average before training, add it back to predict — makes a brand-new user default to the crowd average instead of a useless all-zeros. Try it as a tweak below.

docs.title: 10. The autodiff way — PyTorch
docs.text:
We hand-derived those three gradients. In practice you let automatic differentiation do it: write only the forward cost, call .backward(), and the framework fills in dX, dW, db for you — which is exactly how you'd scale this to millions of users.

Ng's lectures implement this in TensorFlow (tf.GradientTape). We use PyTorch here — it's the industry-standard framework and the idea is identical: define the loss, autodiff gives the gradients, an optimizer steps.

import torch

Yt = torch.tensor(Y, dtype=torch.float32)
Rt = torch.tensor(R, dtype=torch.float32)

# leaf tensors we want gradients for
Xt = (0.1 * torch.randn(n_movies, n)).requires_grad_(True)
Wt = (0.1 * torch.randn(n_users,  n)).requires_grad_(True)
bt = torch.zeros(n_users, requires_grad=True)

opt = torch.optim.Adam([Xt, Wt, bt], lr=0.1)
for epoch in range(2000):
    err  = (Xt @ Wt.T + bt - Yt) * Rt          # the SAME masked error as before
    loss = 0.5 * (err**2).sum() + 0.5 * lam * ((Xt**2).sum() + (Wt**2).sum())
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()                             # autodiff computes every gradient for us
    opt.step()

print("final loss", round(loss.item(), 3))      # matches the from-scratch run

Notice the forward line (Xt @ Wt.T + bt - Yt) * Rt is character-for-character the same as our NumPy E — we just stopped writing the gradients by hand. Swapping in the Adam optimizer (instead of plain fixed-step descent) is why we can use a bigger learning rate and fewer epochs.

docs.title: 11. Your turn
docs.text:
Each is a small tweak to code you already ran — poke at it to build intuition. Try it first; the solution is one click away. Do at least the first two.

1. Reduce to 2 dimensions instead of 1. Change the PCA projection to keep the top two components and confirm the explained-variance ratio now sums to 1.0 (2-D data → 2 axes → nothing lost).

Solution 
W2 = Vt[:2].T                 # keep both components
Z2 = X_c @ W2                 # shape (200, 2) — no reduction, exact
print((s**2 / (s**2).sum())[:2].sum())   # → 1.0
X_recon2 = Z2 @ W2.T + X.mean(axis=0)
print(np.mean((X - X_recon2)**2))        # ≈ 0: reconstruction is exact

2. Confirm the two PCA routes agree. Print the PC1 axis from the covariance/eigen route and from the SVD route side by side — same direction (possibly sign-flipped)?

Solution 
print("eigen PC1:", eig_vecs[:, 0])
print("svd   PC1:", Vt[0])
# same line; if signs are opposite that's the harmless sign ambiguity
print("aligned:", np.allclose(np.abs(eig_vecs[:, 0]), np.abs(Vt[0])))

3. Starve the recommender of data. Drop the observed fraction from 0.4 to 0.15 (regenerate R and Y), retrain, and watch the held-out RMSE climb — fewer known cells, harder to fill the blanks.

Solution 
R = (rng.random((n_movies, n_users)) < 0.15).astype(float)
Y = full * R
X = rng.standard_normal((n_movies, n)) * 0.1
W = rng.standard_normal((n_users,  n)) * 0.1
b = np.zeros(n_users)
for _ in range(3000):
    E = (predict(X, W, b) - Y) * R
    X -= eta * (E @ W + lam * X)
    W -= eta * (E.T @ X + lam * W)
    b -= eta * E.sum(axis=0)
P = predict(X, W, b)
print("held-out RMSE:", np.sqrt(np.mean((P - full)[R == 0]**2)))  # worse than before

4. Add mean normalization. Subtract each movie's observed-rating mean before training and add it back when predicting — the lecture's fix so a no-ratings user defaults to the crowd average, not zero.

Solution 
counts = R.sum(axis=1)
mu = np.where(counts > 0, Y.sum(axis=1) / np.maximum(counts, 1), 0)   # per-movie mean
Yn = (Y - mu[:, None]) * R           # center the observed ratings
# ...train X, W, b on Yn exactly as before...
pred = predict(X, W, b) + mu[:, None]   # add the mean back to predict
# a brand-new (all-zero) user now predicts mu — each movie's average — not 0

5. Overfit with too many latent features. Bump n from 3 to 12 (the true rank is only 3) and compare train vs. held-out RMSE — the gap widens as the extra factors memorize noise.

Solution 
n = 12
X = rng.standard_normal((n_movies, n)) * 0.1
W = rng.standard_normal((n_users,  n)) * 0.1
b = np.zeros(n_users)
for _ in range(3000):
    E = (predict(X, W, b) - Y) * R
    X -= eta * (E @ W + lam * X)
    W -= eta * (E.T @ X + lam * W)
    b -= eta * E.sum(axis=0)
P = predict(X, W, b)
print("train", round(np.sqrt(np.mean((P-full)[R==1]**2)), 3),
      "held", round(np.sqrt(np.mean((P-full)[R==0]**2)), 3))   # bigger gap → turn up lam

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
• Géron, Hands-On ML with Scikit-Learn and PyTorch (2025), Ch. 8 "Dimensionality Reduction" — the PCA-via-SVD treatment Part I is built on, plus the explained-variance elbow, choosing n_components by target variance, and reconstruction error.
  • Raschka et al., ML with PyTorch and Scikit-Learn (2022), Ch. 5 — PCA from scratch the covariance-matrix way: standardize → np.cov → np.linalg.eig/eigh → sort eigenpairs → build the projection matrix W → transform. The mirror of Route A.
  • Recommenders / matrix factorization — not in either book; Part II follows Ng's C3 W2 lectures directly. For more, look up "matrix factorization for recommender systems" (the Netflix-Prize-era technique) and PyTorch nn.Embedding-based implementations.
  • Ng's optional labs, C3W2 — the PCA notebook and the collaborative-filtering assignment, which uses the same masked-cost gradient descent in TensorFlow.
